#126565. Magnus Ditlev Tells Us How He Traded Calamity in Kona for Glory in Florida

📅 13 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 12m • 📚 Deep Dive (2498 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Triathlete ↗ Open Full Page

Magnus Ditlev Tells Us How He Traded Calamity in Kona for Glory in Florida

📅 13 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 12 min read (2498 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Triathlete

⏱️ ~12 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that magnus Ditlev finishes 2026 Ironman Florida in the fastest time at the full distance.
  • How we reported this: Triathlete contributor Travis Mundell interviewed Magnus Ditlev following the Dane’s fastest Ironman time of 7:19:17 at Ironman Florida to hear about what his training looked like after a DNF in Kona one month prior.
  • Industry observers note that thirty years after Lothar Leder became the first person to go under the eight-hour barrier at the full distance, Magnus Ditlev (DEN) set a new fastest-ever time of seven hours and 19 minutes at Ironman Florida.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that magnus Ditlev finishes 2026 Ironman Florida in the fastest time at the full distance. (Photo: Ironman).

How we reported this: Triathlete contributor Travis Mundell interviewed Magnus Ditlev following the Dane’s fastest Ironman time of 7:19:17 at Ironman Florida to hear about what his training looked like after a DNF in Kona one month prior.

Industry observers note that thirty years after Lothar Leder became the first person to go under the eight-hour barrier at the full distance, Magnus Ditlev (DEN) set a new fastest-ever time of seven hours and 19 minutes at Ironman Florida. Ditlev’s performance is even more impressive given it came just one month after imploding and pulling out roughly 30 minutes from a likely Ironman World Championship victory. But does it feel like retribution for the 29-year-old?

“What happened in Kona is still very much in my mind, and I’m probably thinking more about what happened in Kona right now than the world record, to be honest, because that was my significant shot at a world championship title there, and being so close was very heartbreaking,” he told Triathlete, just days after his headline-grabbing race in Florida.

It has been revealed that after finishing second at the Hawaii Ironman World Championship in 2024 and then winning Ironman South Africa in early 2025, Ditlev struggled to consistently reach the level that those performances suggest. And when a bout of shingles early in 2026 left him on the sidelines ahead of Ironman Texas, it seemed as if another season was in jeopardy.

“I wasn’t in a good space because of all the sickness, and I think that was maybe still in the body somehow. Even though I was training OK, I wasn’t performing at races. And when I had to really push, I wasn’t able to do so,” Ditlev noted, of his 11th-place finish at Ironman Frankfurt, where he narrowly secured a Kona qualifying slot. A sixth-place finish at Roth immediately followed, in a race where Sam Laidlow stopped the clock at a world’s best time of 7:21:04.

“That was hard to watch, especially because I was in the race, and I got absolutely humiliated in the race that has given me the most throughout my career, so that was really tough.”.

(Now that Ditlev has the record once more, Laidlow has since teased on Instagram that he is back in training to reclaim it).

Still, seeing the level of the competition gave Ditlev something to take away from the experience.

“Being in that race and seeing the level of Sam and the level of Kristian, it was good to get that kick in the butt,” he mentioned. “That gave me that last little bit of motivation and push to try to get better.”.

Despite that added motivation, returning to the standards Ditlev had set for himself didn’t come without uncertainty.

“There were doubts every day, to be honest. I was doubting basically every step I took along the road, but I didn’t, or very rarely did I, change the aims because of those doubts.”.

That ability to stay the course is something he looks back on with pride.

In a recent development, “That’s one of the things I’m proud of the most – that I never really veered off too much from that plan. I just tried to really work hard and do my best.”.

Sticking to the plan slowly began to pay off behind the scenes: Ditlev headed to altitude in Nederland, Colorado, as he had before Kona in 2024 for his final training block. Finally, he saw some of the best training numbers of his career appearing across the swim, bike, and run.

Industry observers note that “It was so simple where we were staying. It was just me, my girlfriend, and a coach some of the time, and we were just really focused on all the small things and living a simple life,” he explained. “I think going a bit away and not having too much to focus on apart from training and really trying to prepare for a good performance was definitely the thing I needed at that time.”.

Sources indicate that and for most of the race in Kona, those training numbers translated into exactly the performance he had hoped for. Ditlev led off the bike and maintained a commanding lead of more than four minutes throughout the run before his race unraveled under the heat and humidity in the final miles. Seemingly out of nowhere, he found himself seated on a barrier on the Queen K, having come so close to achieving his biggest goal.

Physically turning things around to race another Ironman in Florida in four weeks’ time was one type of challenge; mentally overcoming such a blow was another. Instead of returning home to Denmark, he flew back to Boulder, Colorado, to recover and restart training.

“To be honest, it was quite tough. I had some days where I was really struggling to get out of the door because I was not really motivated and really had to push myself just to get out on the bike and ride,” he shared.

He acknowledged that it took more than his own resolve to get back out training.

Industry observers note that “It was just the people around me that were so supportive, and they were trying to tell me that: ‘Yeah, look, you’re in amazing shape. If you manage to put yourself up to it mentally, then we think you can do amazing in Florida.”’.

At the same time, there was a physical concern in the back of everyone’s mind: whether the effects of the heat stress would linger — knowing Ditlev had gone deep into the well and far into the notoriously brutal 140-mile race.

Industry observers note that “You hear those horror stories of people that have had heat injuries; they are out for long periods, and it could really sit in the system for a long time. So we were quite careful the first couple of days with the training to make sure that I was recovered, and then just didn’t do too much training in between [Kona and Florida].”.

Ditlev moved toward Florida with a lower total training volume, keeping a few bigger, specific sessions while focusing mainly on arriving fresh.

It worked, and the shape was still there. However, that freshness didn’t translate into race-day excitement. Instead, he was focused on qualifying for Kona and earning another chance to put things right.

“I wasn’t too hyped up on the race as I’ve been before Kona, where I’m really looking forward to it so much. Whereas here I was just really relaxed. I think I knew I was in great shape and I wanted to execute, but I was not stressed or nervous that sometimes you can be before substantial races.”.

The day began perfectly for Ditlev. One of the best swims of his career even saw him briefly take the lead after the Australian exit heading into the second lap.

“When you have that swim, for me, then I know it’s gonna be a good day. It felt super easy and relaxed.”.

That set the tone for the rest of the race.

In a recent development, “I just felt like I was not working really hard the whole day, and that was the same for the bike and run. I was just doing my own race in control.”.

Industry observers note that that feeling of “not working really hard” produced the fastest bike split in Ironman history, averaging 29.3 mph — a number age groupers can’t even comprehend for an Olympic-distance race, let alone a full Ironman. To almost any age-group athlete, flying through the course in peak shape would sound like pure bliss. For Ditlev, it brought another sensation.

According to recent reports, “It was quite boring, to be honest, because it was a one-loop course and I didn’t see anyone at all. There was not even a motorbike or anything because the race wasn’t broadcast. So it was super lonely out there. I just tried to make time go by.”.

Sources indicate that thankfully for him, time went by promptly whether he felt it or not. Averaging 345 watts without dropping off power toward the end, he arrived in T2 with a 3:51:16 bike split and an 11-minute gap over the American chasers, including Sam Long, Rudy von Berg, and Ben Kanute.

After that swim and bike, Ditlev knew the fastest Ironman time was within reach. Before starting the run, he asked his girlfriend what marathon time he needed to secure it.

“I thought, ‘I can definitely do that, given how I’m feeling.’”.

Recent findings suggest that recounting the moment, Ditlev laughed as he described briefly debating whether to chase the record or take it easy with such an immense lead. Once again, the prospect of it being “too boring” helped him decide to “at least make the effort.”.

Industry observers note that starting at 3:35 per kilometer, or 5:46 per mile, he described the run as feeling “really smooth” until the final 8K, when he had to slow slightly. In the end, he still finished with a career-best 2:33:31 marathon. Despite that, and a upcoming world’s best time, the specter of the Big Island tempered his elation.

“It’s probably because of Kona, but I wasn’t too hyped or too excited because it’s also in the back of my mind. This is what should have happened in Hawaii. So it’s a bit of a weird feeling.”.

One of the biggest headline pieces of gear Ditlev debuted in Kona was his newly introduced, full-face-covering visor, which returned in Florida. Beyond its appearance, some questioned its practicality, wondering whether it would make the heat harder to manage. Ditlev quickly dismissed that concern, saying, “It doesn’t make a significant difference in how hot I feel.”.

But it wasn’t the visor that stole the attention in Florida; the biggest question about his setup was the lump in the center of his chest, with many speculating that it was some sort of newly introduced cooling strategy.

In a recent development, “It’s not for cooling. It’s just been a long time since I did a smaller Ironman race, and I found out there are no personal needs or pro fluids like there are in Kona, Roth, and Frankfurt that I’ve done this year.”.

The explanation was more practical than it looked.

“So I was having a hard time figuring out how I should carry my nutrition around the course. So actually, it’s just two 500 milliliter bottles with all my nutrition for the run.”.

After seeing the footage, however, he acknowledged the unusual appearance.

“It feels pretty natural, even though when I saw the videos, I can obviously see that it looks quite stupid.”.

Recent findings suggest that when you’re aiming for 200 grams of carbohydrate per hour on the bike, and 150-160 grams on the run, carrying the nutrition took priority over appearances. But these insane grams-per-hour levels weren’t even the highest intake his team tested.

“We did some tests with 220 actually, and it’s not the ceiling. It’s just becoming a diminishing return, if you can say it that way,” he explained. “I could probably add some more, but we are starting to go into really small potential benefits, and the consequences of it going wrong, or the risks, start to outweigh the potential rewards.”.

Industry observers note that A performance like this makes it easy to imagine Ditlev as a childhood triathlon prodigy. Yet just 10 years ago, he was competing in his first age-group triathlon, with his only athletic background in football and badminton. Asked what he would tell that younger, 19-year-old Magnus, he laughed.

Recent findings suggest that “Age-group Magnus didn’t even know that there was actually something called professional Ironman racing,” he noted, before continuing, “Make sure that you are enjoying what you’re doing. If I didn’t enjoy it, I wouldn’t be doing it now. So just try to surround yourself with people that give you energy and stay curious about the process.”.

His latest time also raises an inevitable question: How much faster can he go?

First, Ditlev promptly kept the story straight: “It’s fun to set a fast time, but we are racing for wins,” before entertaining the thought experiment.

According to recent reports, “I don’t know if Florida is the fastest course in the world. It’s definitely a fast course. But some years it has been a wetsuit; then you are at least two minutes, maybe even three minutes quicker. Then, if you apply the transition zone that they have in Roth, which is something like four or five minutes quicker combined T2 time and T1, then we are somewhere between seven and eight minutes just from that.”.

The bike offered another potential saving.

“My bike engineer actually had me at 3:48 bike split before the race, but the wind conditions weren’t ideal on race day. So if you take a day with no wind, then I would probably be around 3:48, which is another three minutes. So then we are at about 10 minutes.”.

On the run, he had a wry smile as he pointed to third-place finisher Matt Hanson’s 2:28 marathon, not suggesting he could go that fast; he believed he could still squeeze out “a little bit more.”.

“I mean, probably 10 minutes, quite easily, quicker.”.

For now, Ditlev is finally spending some time at home in Denmark after an extended stretch away. Not everyone embraces the off-season quite so readily – we’re looking at you, Taylor Knibb – but Ditlev indicates he is known among those close to him for being able to switch from some of the biggest training hours in the sport to almost none in a short space of time.

Amid the downtime, the fire still burns for a Kona title, with middle-distance and Ironman Pro Series racing taking a back seat to his preference for building toward specific goals.

Asked whether he wishes he could have a rematch against the now-retired Kona champion Vincent Luis, his answer was clear.

It has been revealed that “Of course. You want to beat the best people, and Vince was the best athlete in Kona that day. And I have to admit, when I saw that Vince was the guy that passed me first after I almost collapsed, I thought, ‘Okay, that’s actually pretty cool if he goes ahead and wins this race.’”.

Having spent time with Luis at altitude earlier in the year, Ditlev was happy to see him take the title off into retirement, even if it means missing the chance to race him again.

“He’s a really, really good guy, so I was super happy for him. And I thought it’s gonna be absolutely epic if he manages to keep it to the line. But yeah, of course, I’m sad that he’s retiring. It would be nice to race him next year as well.”.

“Have I never had an original experience?”.

Recent findings suggest that chances are you’ve seen this exact question written in the comments section on social media. There’s relief in being able to relate to other people’s silly, honest, or otherwise unfiltered life moments, because you start to realize that you’re not alone. You’re human.

You could say that yoga teachers have their own version of the “perfectly normal” trend. It’s perfectly normal for yoga teachers to be completely imperfect. And isn’t embracing your mistakes exactly what yoga encourages us to do, anyway? If you’ve had your fair share of slip ups, quirks, and completely unserious moments as a yoga teacher, consider yourself part of the club.

#126560. The 12 Best Carbon Plate Shoes for Setting PRs, Running Your First Marathon, and Crossing the Finish Line Upright

The 12 Best Carbon Plate Shoes for Setting PRs, Running Your First Marathon, and Crossing the Finish Line Upright

📅 07 Jun 2023 | ⏱️ 20 min read (3941 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Runnersworld

⏱️ ~20 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that we earn a commission for products purchased through some links in this article.
  • Recent findings suggest that there are several max-cushioned shoes we recommend to carry you through hours of pounding pavement, but the true titans—composed of super foams sandwiching carbon-fiber plates—are listed here.
  • Sources indicate that in 2017, Nike shook up running as we knew it with the unveiling of its Vaporfly 4%, a carbon plate marathon racing shoe that promised a 4 percent improvement in running economy (the measure of how fast you run based on the level of oxygen you use).
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that we earn a commission for products purchased through some links in this article. Why Trust Us?

Recent findings suggest that there are several max-cushioned shoes we recommend to carry you through hours of pounding pavement, but the true titans—composed of super foams sandwiching carbon-fiber plates—are listed here. There’s also a slew of new super shoes that made their debut this marathon cycle. We’ll update accordingly once these racers are available.

Sources indicate that in 2017, Nike shook up running as we knew it with the unveiling of its Vaporfly 4%, a carbon plate marathon racing shoe that promised a 4 percent improvement in running economy (the measure of how fast you run based on the level of oxygen you use). Today, almost every shoe brand has a super shoe with a carbon plate and super foams, and they all make the same promise as the Vaporfly 4%: less energy expenditure while racing, or the ability to run faster with the same effort.

It has been revealed that here, we list the top performers based on wear-tester feedback and our own experiences racing in them. And if you’re in the market for other shoes to help you with your training, we have a buying guide for those too.

Your first marathon → Adidas Adizero Adios Pro 5 (Men’s/Women’s)For a PR → Nike Alphafly 4 (Men’s/Women’s)But want to train in a plated shoe → New Balance SC Rebel (Men’s/Women’s)A flat and fast course → Saucony Endorphin Elite 3 (Unisex)A half marathon → Asics Metaspeed Edge Tokyo (Unisex)And want to try low drop → Altra Vanish Carbon 3 (Men’s/Women’s)And need support → Saucony Endorphin Pro 5 (Men’s/Women’s)And have wide feet → Hoka Cielo X1 3.0 (Unisex)On a track → Puma Fast-R Nitro Elite 3 (Men’s/Women’s)A 5K or 10K → New Balance SuperComp Elite v6 (Men’s/Women’s)On a trail → Hoka Tecton X 4 (Men’s/Women’s)An ultra → On Cloudultra Pro (Men’s/Women’s).

In a recent development, besides our local testers, some of whom have been testing for us for the past 15 years, and staff who’ve also logged their share of road and trail time in these shoes, I have tested several of these shoes on race days. I have run 28 marathons since 2010, including 14 consecutive Boston Marathons. And I have made the split-second decision to race in newly introduced shoes marathon morning.

According to recent reports, I’ve spoken with brand shoe development teams and have kept up with the latest super shoe releases. Upcoming shoes not listed here are still undergoing the testing process and will be added once feedback is in.

Sources indicate that all of the shoes on this list were tested by local runners and Runner’s World staff. Our local testers include 300-plus men and women of various running experience levels, paces, arch heights, and gait patterns. From enthusiasts who run for fun to several Olympic-qualifying hopefuls, our mix of testers rounds out a sample of the overall running pop.

RW editors, including myself, have also raced in these shoes, from 5K to marathon distance (and some ultrarunners). We take into consideration fit, feel, and ride to determine the best racing shoes for almost every kind of runner hoping to PR, or just enjoy the propulsive experience of running on carbon plates sandwiched between super foams.

Sources indicate that on a plane, running a shakeout run, and anytime a marathon was weeks away or days past, I’d hear first-timers and seasoned vets say the Adizero Adios Pro 4 was their race day shoe of choice. The latest iteration is sure to have the same mentions next race cycle.

I didn’t have the chance to race in the Adizero Adios Pro 5 yet, but I did try them out on my usual Central Park circuit in Fresh York City. I was practically racing my casual loop after slurping half a can of beer (it was a long day on the job). It obviously wasn’t the kiwi-flavored Belgian White that had me clocking marathon pace (it got kinda funky after the 25th sip).

The carbon rim, which replaces the 4’s energy rods, is the secret sauce that subtracts weights and encourages a powerful snap that had me run up and down Harlem Hill like a gazelle. The Lightstrike Pro foam is also slightly firmer, which helps with high rebound and stability.

My only knock is how the rim shreds the hell of my ankle if my form gets slow and sloppy. But it’s a character trait. Senior Art Director Colin McSherry, for instance, ran his first marathon and had no challenges—shoe- or first 26.2-related—during his run.

Shop Men’s at adidas.com | Shop Women’s at adidas.com.

Adidas Adizero Adios Pro 5 Review.

In a recent development, the Alphafly 3 went through some major changes to become more inclusive in terms of fit, weight, and ride. How do you enhancement a shoe that was worn by the late Kelvin Kiptum, former marathon world record holder (2:00:35)? It starts with the Air units.

The ones in the Alphafly 4 are lighter and softer. During his testing, Runner-in-Chief Jeff Dengate noted how the unit visibly squishes down when you stomp on the forefoot. The effect is a smoother, comfier ride with lots of pop.

The width of the shoe is also slightly wider (Nike really wants runners to stop saying their shoes are too unstable and narrow). Dengate noted how he didn’t have to slow down when turning corners.

The main critique is that loud clomping sound. But at this point—is it really an Alphafly if you can’t hear it coming up from behind you meters away?

Shop Men’s at nike.com | Shop Women’s at nike.com.

Industry observers note that the jury is still out on the pros and cons of solely training in super shoes, but we’re in the camp of keeping your special trainer fresh for race day. You can get a couple of runs in to troubleshoot and see if there are any complications pre-marathon or half, but I still urge runners to save the magic. But if you can’t get enough of that super foam, carbon plate high, enter the SC Rebel.

Sources indicate that new Balance created this shoe specifically to make your training feel easier. It has the brand’s new TPEE-based Infinion foam, tuned for power runs, just like the SuperComp Elite v6 (New Balance’s premium racing shoe). It’s also an ideal alternative for racing if you need more stability. The shoe has a broader platform and grippy outsole that kept me upright on wet mud during a long run.

Shop Men’s at newbalance.com | Shop Women’s at newbalance.com.

New Balance SuperComp Rebel Review.

Industry observers note that the Endorphin Elite 3 is as squishy and bouncy as its predecessor, but Saucony made the shoe more stable by connecting the forefoot and heel. Turns are less scary, but there’s still a learning curve to master the incredible energy return running in these shoes.

I tested them at a 5K and 3K in the Brooklyn Navy Yard, which was pocked with potholes and patched with slippery gravel. The shoes cut corners, but I still felt the need to slow down—or wipe out. I think on a more controlled runner’s feet these would make her feel powerful and unbeatable.

Sources indicate that the source of that aggressive bounce is the TPEE-based IncrediRun foam. Its ride rivals even PEBA’s energy return.

The shoe also didn’t produce hot spots in the toe area. Saucony seems to have improved the fit with the third version. Once I wield this shoe’s power I won’t be afraid to run longer than a 10K. No friction here.

Shop Endorphin Elite 3 at saucony.com.

Saucony Endorphin Elite 3 Review.

According to recent reports, when I ran the Tokyo Marathon last year, I laced up in the Asics Metaspeed Sky Paris because I wanted more cushioning in the forefoot area. Asics recognized there are two ways of racing: stride running or cadence running. The Sky is intended for stride running: when you have a more powerful gait with longer strides and tend to strike on the midfoot.

Recent findings suggest that at the Sydney Marathon this year, I opted for the Metaspeed Edge Tokyo instead. I felt the Edge would give me the, er, competitive edge, so to speak. My steps per minute are usually more than the average runner due to my mechanics and, well, because I’m short. The shoe has a scooped plate tilted slightly downward to cater to those with shorter steps (cadence running). I ended up hitting my sub-3:10 goal, finishing in 3:05.

It has been revealed that the Edge Tokyo is updated with a softer underfoot, making the shoe more flexible. This makes the shoe have an incredible snap at toe-off. I was able to change gears at a fast clip when I latched onto a runner I was determined to pass (not always the best race strategy, but worked like a charm when I saw male runners try to overtake me).

It has been revealed that where competitors’ shoes have “air pods” or decoupled heels, the Metaspeeds provide runners with a simplified, choose-your-own-adventure super shoe that packs a powerful punch. One note for the wise: Because the Edge Tokyo has less firm cushioning, my heels and arches felt sore postrace. If you have heavy footfalls like me, have those recovery sandals waiting for you at bag check.

Shop Asics Metaspeed Edge Tokyo at amazon.com.

Asics Metaspeed Tokyo Shoes Review.

Sources indicate that altra started its journey into super shoes by staying true to itself. The Vanish Carbon 1 and 2 had wide toeboxes and were zero drop. But the Altra team knew there would have to be a compromise to go up against competitors’ shoes: the Vanish Carbon 3 needed a drop. The brand preserved the Altra way by adding just 4 mm (like the shoes in its Experience collection) to the heel with an aggressive rocker profile to promote propulsion.

Another Altra signature in the shoe is the roomy toebox that gives racers space to splay their toes, allowing them to engage their digits and power up during push-off.

Sources indicate that the third iteration has pure PEBA midsole foam called FastRce. The foam provides more energy return and 2.6 percent improved running economy over the Vanish Carbon 2, which had a PEBA/EVA blend in its midsole.

The overall package presents a racer capable of racing against the other super shoes on this list.

Shop Women’s at altrarunning.com.

The Endorphin Pro 5 has a more stable ride than its springier sibling, the Endorphin Elite 2, which we also included on this list.

It has been revealed that its midsole is dual-layer PEBA, with one layer Pwrrun PB and the other layer Pwrrun HG. These layers provide a high-rebound ride and work with the rocker Speedroll tech to encourage fast, smooth turnover.

Testers like the shoe’s propulsive ride as well as support throughout their workouts.

“What stood out most was the combination of propulsion and stability,” mentioned tester Srah Pezzino. “The carbon plate paired with Saucony’s Pwrrun HG foam delivers a responsive, fast ride without feeling unstable or overly bouncy. This helped immensely during longer tempo runs when fatigue starts to creep in. I felt like the shoe encouraged good mechanics and smooth turnover rather than forcing speed.

According to recent reports, “Compared to previous carbon-plated shoes I’ve worn, the Pro 5 feels more predictable and controlled, especially when my form isn’t perfect late in a run. It’s a shoe that makes you feel fast without punishing you for not being perfectly locked in.”.

Shop Men’s at saucony.com | Shop Women’s at saucony.com.

According to recent reports, the lightest Hoka marathon racing shoe yet is the Cielo X1 3.0, with street cred at the 2025 Chicago Marathon. Hoka-sponsored pro-runner Alex Masai raced in a blacked-out prototype of the shoe, shaved nearly four minutes off his personal best time, and podiumed third with a 2:04:37 finish.

Sources indicate that and our testers clocked the shoe’s massive updates, as well. “The 3.0 is sturdier than the 2.0,” said tester Mike Browne. “I’m referring to the sturdiness mainly on heel strikes. I wore the 2.0 during marathon training and in a marathon, and they actually underpronated a little. I think that is what caused the outside heel rubber to come off on both shoes. The 3.0 has corrected that problem and seems to strike the ground in the center, which makes for a more even wear on the shoe.”.

Besides implementing a lighter upper, the Hoka team redesigned the midsole shape, creating a long channel that runs down the center of the shoe. The rocker also isn’t as exaggerated. What you get is a more stable, smoother ride while racing with propulsion that’s comparable to Hoka’s competitors’. The fit is also broader in the midfoot, making the Cielo X1 3.0 a good choice for runners with wide feet.

Shop Hoka Cielo X1 3 at hoka.com.

The Fast-R Nitro Elite 3 is a prime pick for marathon racing, but it’s also a solid choice for everything else under 26.2 miles. The shoe is so lightweight and delivers such explosive rebound—“you feel like you’re running straight down a trampoline,” says a tester—that it left some of us feeling like we had brownie batter for legs after hard efforts.

Recent findings suggest that the shoe was the talk of the industry prelaunch after Puma released a study (which the brand sponsored) comparing the Fast-R Nitro Elite 3’s performance to the Nike Alphafly 3, Adidas Adios Pro Evo 1, and Puma Fast-R 2. The study claimed the Elite 3 was 3.15 to 3.62 percent more economical than its competitors.

In a recent development, putting those numbers aside, our testers agreed this is one powerful racing shoe. “The foam used in this shoe is very noticeable, even when simply starting with a short warmup in the shoe,” notes tester Codi Januszkiewicz, who compares the ride to the Adidas Adizero Adios Pro 4. “Accelerating from a warmup pace straight into some speedwork intervals felt smooth; somehow moving faster in this shoe felt even easier than the warmup.”.

Recent findings suggest that but that power is a lot to handle. “The stability is lacking,” indicates tester Sean O’Connor. “Almost felt high heelish to me, and it jacked up my calves and feet a little as well. When I ran in them it felt like I was perpetually holding onto the shoe with my feet. I think that's why it made my calves and feet sore.”.

Recent findings suggest that some can handle the shoe’s intensity over a long period of time. Others may assign the Elite 3 as their mid-distance racing shoe instead. I wore the Elite 3 at a Trackmith 5000 meters over the summer, hitting a PR at 19:12. It’s cush in the heel, but judging by my footfalls, which are heavy, I think racing them in a 26.2 would prolong my usual recovery time postrun.

When I raced the 2025 London Marathon, I had been training in the FuelCell SuperComp Elite v4 but instead opted for the FuelCell SuperComp Pacer v2. The Pacer is sleeker and lightweight, unlike the SuperComp Elite v4, which was too beefy for my small frame. The SuperComp Elite v6 is the version of the shoe I would have raced in. Unfortunately, I can’t go back to April 2025. Fortunately for you, the Elite v6 is here just in time for fall marathon season.

Recent findings suggest that the shoe features the brand’s Infinion foam, which was introduced in the 1080v15. The Elite v6’s version of the TPEE- and TPU-based foam is dialed-in for race-ready energy return.

It has been revealed that I took the shoe out on a track for a 2 x 2-mile workout at 6:45 pace and the shoes handled turns and helped me hit goal pace. The ride isn’t as aggressive as the Saucony Endorphin Elite 3 or Alphafly, and the cushioning is firmer. Runners with an efficient stride and good form can get away with running marathons and halfs in these shoes, but I’d recommend these for 5Ks and 10Ks because of the firmness and less explosive rebound. The lighter weight makes it ideal for track and medium-distance road races.

Shop Men’s at newbalance.com | Shop Women’s at newbalance.com.

Latest Balance SuperComp Elite v6 Review.

Though I’ve been racing for 20 years, nothing will get me running an ultra on the trail—which is where our Senior Editor Cat Bowen comes in. Bowen conquered scrambles on steep climbs, dusty ridgelines, gnarly technical trails, and more types of terrain than I run in a year, while testing the long-awaited Tecton X 4.

It has been revealed that she gave a shoutout to the hardy Matryx upper that’s “tough as nails” and the grippy 4mm lugs that prevented her from plunging forward. The plus/minus with the shoe is that built-in gaiter collar. Bowen appreciated the extra coverage, but lamented how difficult it was to put on the shoe (we get it: a side zipper would be a good cheat but adds weight). “There is absolutely no reason why this shoe has a front pull tab and nothing in the back,” she wrote in her review.

According to recent reports, still, the fresh cushioning, Hoka’s ProFly X, and non-winged plate make for a more energized ride that’s less rigid without losing stability. It’s a great shoe for unpredictable. but Bowen urges you to not go the no-sock route.

Shop Men’s at hoka.com | Shop Women’s at hoka.com.

Recent findings suggest that for hours, days, weeks on the trail, there’s the Cloudultra Pro. Bowen has gone through three pairs of the shoe—not because they lack durability but because she likes them so much and runs that much—and appreciates how she doesn’t have to slice the sides. Feet swell during ultras, but it sounds like On prepared for that with its roomy but secure upper.

According to recent reports, another plus in Bowen’s column of ultra shoe musts is the Cloudultra Pro’s lateral stability. Maneuvering over rugged, uneven terrain could spell twisted ankles and slipping and sliding, but the shoe didn’t lead Bowen astray.

Ultrarunner Pat Heine-Holmberg also wore the shoe around Germany’s Zugspitze, where he raced the 102-mile ZUT1000 and ran on “every surface imaginable.”.

Shop Men’s at on.com | Shop Women’s at on.com.

It has been revealed that brands are now beginning to release carbon shoes in men’s and women’s sizes. Still, in some cases there’s not much difference between the types of shoes except for maybe the sizing and colors. If the shoes are unisex, it may take a few try-ons to get the fit right. In my unisex racing shoe experience, I’ve found the collar can be loose while the midfoot can be tight. You may want to size up or down, and adopt the heel-lock tying method if the heel area feels too loose.

Do all carbon-fiber plates behave the same way? Sort of. An vital lesson to learn here is that the plate isn’t the secret sauce of super shoes—it doesn’t cause propulsion. Instead, the plate, sandwiched between the highly responsive foams, acts as a stabilizer to the super foam. This is why super shoes have such tall stack heights, and why World Athletics caps racing shoe stack height at 40 mm. The super foam—and amount underfoot—is a major advantage.

When choosing a carbon-plate shoe, you’ll want to consider what you’re using it for—racing on the road or trail—and, if possible, have your gait evaluated to determine the best plate angle if you’re looking at shoes specific to running type.

Some plates are full-length or have cutouts. In shoes like the Asics Metaspeed Edge and Metaspeed Sky, the plate’s angle differentiates running types. The Edge’s plate dips lower in the forefoot so cadence runners can roll off their toes faster. The Sky’s plate sits flat in the forefoot, allowing stride runners to leverage bounce on longer steps.

According to recent reports, the secret sauce in super shoes is the foam. PEBA (polyether block amide) was once considered the holy grail of all foams and you can still find it in most super shoes, but newer models are using TPEE (thermoplastic polyester elastomer) and A-TPU (aliphatic thermoplastic polyurethane) because they’re more resistant to bottoming out, or going flat. The ride is more durable—and can be quite aggressively bouncy and squishy.

To truly gauge which foam is best for you, trying on the shoe and giving it a run (preferably with some cornering) will help you determine if you want a firmer or squishier ride.

In a recent development, A carbon-fiber plate shoe is an investment, costing anywhere from $240 upward of $500. There are a couple of things to take into account on a personal level before buying: Can you afford a trainer that’s less durable compared to the standard workhorse shoe, which lasts between 450 to 500 miles?

Sources indicate that while these super shoes are more durable than the ones made eight years ago, they still have a shorter shelf life due to high-performance foams—PEBA and supercritical blends—wearing down faster. Lastly, is the return there? While brands claim these shoes can improve performance, it’s not guaranteed your running economy will improve by around 4 percent.

I spoke with Ted Fitzpatrick, Saucony’s VP of product management, about the differences. He made these key points between carbon and nylon plates:.

Sources indicate that A nylon plate is semirigid with some flexibility. A carbon plate is rigid with little or no flexibility. Popsicle analogy—Imagine the plate as the stick that holds the soft ice cream together. The fundamental use of the plates is to keep the dimensional stability of the foam. With each type of plate, each offers different levels of compliance. The plate maintains the forward rolling effect of super shoes. Carbon is the stiffest, which offers the most concentrated effect of speed roll technology. Nylon still adds stiffness, however, it offers better compliance in how the foot transitions in the gait cycle. Some individuals can respond better to different plates. It is down to what works best for the user.

Saucony offers the nylon-plated Endorphin Speed 6, a training shoe that complements its racer, the Endorphin Pro. The shoe can also serve as a more affordable racing shoe, at $180. (The Endorphin Elite 3 and Endorphin Pro 5 cost $290 and $240.).

“The foam is what does the heavy lifting of a super shoe, however it’s the plate that guides how each foam behaves to the user,” says Fitzpatrick. “It is best to train in both to strengthen and build ‘muscle memory’ into different muscle groups.”.

However, we wouldn’t recommend solely training in super shoes. For one thing, it would be extremely expensive to use these shoes as daily trainers when they have a shorter shelf life compared to standard everyday shoes. We advise going on a couple of runs before racing in the shoes, to get used to running in them and check for hot spots. While running constantly in these shoes won’t necessarily lead to injury, overuse and the desire to run faster in carbon shoes will likely lead to getting sidelined if you’re not careful.

In a recent development, amanda Furrer, Editor, Running Reviews, studied journalism at NYU and writing at Emerson College. She has reviewed gear and covered other topics in the running space for almost 10 years. Since 2013, she has consecutively run the Boston Marathon. She also has a master’s degree in gastronomy from Boston University and was formerly a professional baker for two years before hanging up her apron.

Isakova and Hidalgo Win Final WTCS Races in Abu Dhabi, Jorgensen Podiums

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

(Photo: Wagner Araujo/World Triathlon).

The postponed WTCS Abu Dhabi brought the World Triathlon Championship Series, as it is right now known, to a close ahead of its transition to T50 racing within the Triathlon World Tour. The sprint-distance showdown still attracted many of the sport’s top names, with Olympic qualification points and the chance to finish the season on a high and build momentum into 2027.

Industry observers note that the top spot on the podium was wide open in the women’s race, with the series’ undefeated champion Cassandre Beaugrand (FRA) absent. Add to the mix the shorter, sprint-distance format and hot, windy conditions set to play a factor, and it was anyone’s guess who would take it.

2025 world champion Lisa Tertsch (GER) was the substantial name going in, alongside Jeanne Lehair (LUX), who had been part of a sprint finish at the World Cup in Hong Kong the week before. However, Diana Isakova (RUS) was another athlete many had their eyes on after winning that sprint against Lehair and taking the World Cup win in Rome before that. American Gwen Jorgensen (USA) had shown glimmers of top form in recent races, placing fifth at WTCS Weihai and producing the second-fastest run split at the Grand Final in Pontevedra.

Into the warm, 82-degree water, three groups began to form near the front as the chop and currents made for one of the most difficult swims of the year.

Isakova and Lehair were among the first group out of the water, while Tertsch and Jorgensen exited more than 20 seconds behind. That deficit would rapidly balloon to over 30 seconds early on the bike, with another group between them and the front of the race.

Halfway through the bike, the front group of nine maintained its advantage as the third group swallowed the second to form one large chase pack. On such a tight, technical course, the larger group offered little additional benefit as the smaller pack ahead steadily increased its lead.

At the end of the bike, Germany’s Laura Lindemann (GER) almost undid the work of the front, mishandling her bike after the dismount, almost causing a crash. Onto the run, a quick transition shot Isakova to the front, while around 36 seconds behind, Jorgensen and Tertsch were among the large group with significant work to do – and only 5km to do it.

In a recent development, by halfway, Isakova and Lehair were clear at the front, foreshadowing a repeat of the race in Hong Kong the week prior. Jorgensen remained 36 seconds behind but had gapped Tertsch and made her way into eighth place.

Sources indicate that that momentum continued for Jorgensen as suddenly eighth place became third and she could see the leaders up ahead. Unfortunately, the gap was just too large at that point. Isakova made her move with over 200 meters to go, picking up her first WTCS win and cementing her remarkable end to the year.

Lehair finished second and reflected that her efforts on the bike may have affected her run: “I may have used too much energy, but I am super happy with second place and my third podium of the year.”.

Jorgensen couldn’t believe her result, returning to the WTCS podium for the first time since 2016 at 40 years old and producing the fastest run split of the day.

“I thought I was out of this race but one of the coaches told me I was third and I couldn’t believe it,” she shared.

It has been revealed that in the men’s race, this year’s Grand Final winner and sprint-distance specialist Matt Hauser (AUS) was wearing bib #1. With his prowess in the water, all eyes were on him in the absence of latest world champion Vasco Vilaça (POR). Brazil’s Miguel Hidalgo (BRA), meanwhile, was looking to finally turn his training form into a result after some disappointing recent outings.

Recent findings suggest that fresh Zealand’s Hayden Wilde (NZL) was the other big name on the lineup, having recently been approved to race both WTCS Abu Dhabi and Dubai T100. With the races falling within 24 hours of each other, that would not normally be allowed under World Triathlon rules. With his eyes firmly back on the Olympics, this was Wilde’s A-race for the weekend, according to New Zealand’s National Performance Manager Stephen Sheldrake.

It started with a windy, choppy swim that mostly stayed compact until the return to the beach, when two lines formed toward the shore. One group, including Hauser, made a beeline for the beach to get out of the water as soon as possible and run along the shore toward transition. That worked well for the Australian, who entered T1 with a small gap over compatriot Luke Willian (AUS).

In a recent development, wilde found himself 39 seconds in arrears, with work to do alongside recent Iquique World Cup winner David Cantero del Campo (ESP). They were in a large chase group aiming to gain time on the lead group of 11, but on such a short, fast, five-lap bike course, their work was cut out for them.

Sources indicate that almost immediately, however, the gap was nearly cut in half, with Wilde driving the chase to within 22 seconds by the end of the first lap. The pace was so hot that the group split apart, with only a few athletes able to go with him on the technical course.

Perhaps that woke up the front group, which managed to limit its losses over the remainder of the bike and reached T2 with around nine seconds on Wilde and organization. It was less than they would have hoped for against the stellar Kiwi runner, but the major question was whether the bike had stung his legs enough to hold him off. A slow transition from the 2025 winner of this race gave him even more work to do.

Onto the run, it didn’t take long for Hauser and Hidalgo to separate themselves at the front. Behind them, Wilde promptly recovered from his transition losses and moved through the rest of the front group alongside Shachar Sagiv (ISR).

It has been revealed that the front two continued to push the pace and began adding time to Wilde behind. Hidalgo made his move before the second lap, and Hauser wasn’t able to respond. He quickly began to lose ground as the Brazilian looked comfortable all the way to the finish, taking the tape with an unmatched 14:20 5km.

In a recent development, it was a much-needed WTCS win to carry momentum into the 2027 Triathlon World Tour. Hauser shared afterward that he “could really feel the legs – and the whole year – in the back end of that race.”.

In a recent development, wilde crossed the line in third, comfortably ahead of the rest of the field, but a 14:52 5km left him short of the run speed he is accustomed to producing in these races. He won’t have much time to digest the result, however, as he immediately has to travel to Dubai, where he would look to continue his dominant T100 season.

⁠Before You Spend on Gravel Suspension, Try Wider Tubeless Tires for a Simpler, Smoother Ride

📅 07 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1054 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Bicycling

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review.
  • According to recent reports, just the other day a friend getting into gravel was asking me about suspension parts for his relatively latest gravel bike.
  • When I ran a shop I installed plenty of suspension parts on bikes for people who felt it was the only way they could be more comfortable on the bike.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review. We may earn commission if you buy from a link. How we test gear.

According to recent reports, just the other day a friend getting into gravel was asking me about suspension parts for his relatively latest gravel bike. He was considering different suspension components as a means to gain comfort while he rides—especially on chunkier gravel. He mentioned his frame isn’t compatible with a suspension fork, but was looking at parts like a suspension stem and suspension seatpost. If this sounds like you read this before hitting add to cart on those parts.

When I ran a shop I installed plenty of suspension parts on bikes for people who felt it was the only way they could be more comfortable on the bike. Certain riders fit the bill for a suspension seat post or suspension stem. A few customers had prostate problems and a suspension seat post helped them stay on the bike longer. Others had wrist or hand issues and they benefited from a suspension stem. But even those riders could get additional comfort from a simple change.

Sources indicate that after trying all the suspension components I could add to my own bike (as well as trying a full-suspension gravel bike), I have realized that throwing suspension at a gravel bike doesn’t necessarily fix the concern of being more comfortable on the ride. In the shop, customers would ask about installing a suspension fork on a hybrid or gravel bike, but not all frames are even compatible with a suspension fork.

Adding suspension parts to the bike can change the overall feel of the bike, not to mention the weight those parts typically add. When riders are looking for more comfort on their gravel bike the component swap I pick first is simple—wider tires. Here we’ll talk about the benefits of wider tires and why going tubeless gives your ride that extra bit of cush.

According to recent reports, step one of getting more comfortable on your gravel bike is setting up your tires as tubeless if they aren’t already set up that way. Tubeless systems allow you to run your pressure lower compared to running tubes, which in combination with a wider tire offers more comfort. Running tubes with a lower tire pressure leaves you susceptible to pinch flats, but tubeless systems remove the tubes from the equation.

According to recent reports, one easy way to check if your tires are set up as tubeless is to loosen the nut at the bottom of your valve and gently press it into the rim. If you press it in and air starts to come out, then tighten the nut back up—congratulations, your tires are set up as tubeless!

Industry observers note that if they aren’t tubeless, then it’s time to check compatibility. Check the specs of your bike to see if your rim and tire are tubeless-compatible. If they aren’t you’ll have to explore new wheel and tire options, but if they’re compatible you can convert them to tubeless. Some bikes come stock with tubeless-compatible rims and tires, but don’t come set up tubeless out of the box. Tubeless systems require specific rim tape or rim strips to properly set them up. I’ve seen plenty of bikes come with tubes installed, but with rims taped with tubeless tape. Again, check your individual bike’s specs to see if this includes your bike.

According to recent reports, if you need to pull the tubes out of your tubeless-compatible wheels and tires, then you’ll need a few things. First is a good set of tubeless valves. My favorite are Muc-Off Tubeless Valves. They come with a valve core remover tool on the valve cap, come in different lengths depending on your rim depth, and there are a myriad of colors to add a little pop to your bike. You’ll also need tubeless sealant. I’ve tested more sealants than I can remember, but the tried-and-true sealant I go back to is Stan’s Sealant. Tara Seplavy, Bicycling’s Deputy Editor, walks through setting up your tubeless tires here.

It has been revealed that A bike rarely comes stock with the widest tire that fits in the bike. For example, the Trek Checkpoint SL5 is equipped with 700x42mm, but can fit up to 700x50mm tires when there are no fenders on the bike. Always check the technical specifications for your specific make and model to see how wide you can go. Over the last few years, bike manufacturers have been pushing the envelope to allow for wider and wider tires on bikes. If you have a previous model-year bike that doesn’t mean you can bank on the current model’s tire clearance fitting your bike. Be sure to check the correct generation for your specific make and model. If you go with a tire wider than the maximum width for your bike, you risk damaging the fork and frame.

On my own gravel rig, I recently bumped from 700x40mm tires to 700x45mm tires and noticed the difference immediately. I stuck with the same tire make and model—the Pirelli Cinturato H. The extra five millimeters of width immediately gave more comfort and traction on chunkier gravel and some local singletrack; even with the same tire tread. Five millimeters might not sound like a lot, but it added significant comfort while putting out rides longer than one hundred miles.

Wider tires are the right choice for many—even if you aren’t pushing your mileage into the triple digits. Recently I bumped up the tire width on my dad’s gravel bike. Adding wider tires to his bike (as well as a slightly thicker handlebar tape) leveled up his comfort level while riding. Whether you are taking your gravel bike on singletrack, chunky gravel, hundred-mile rides, or just want a little more comfort on your local lunch loop, go tubeless and bump up your tire width.

Lately though, his toughest balancing act has been fitting trainer rides between family life and the next adventure.

Latest Update: The 9 Best Stability Shoes for Every Type of Runner

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that we earn a commission for products purchased through some links in this article.
  • Sources indicate that editor’s Note, November 17, 2026: The Brooks Adrenaline GTS 25 is currently our “Best Overall” choice.
  • Some shoes do not have a sexy reputation.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that we earn a commission for products purchased through some links in this article. Why Trust Us?

Sources indicate that editor’s Note, November 17, 2026: The Brooks Adrenaline GTS 25 is currently our “Best Overall” choice. Recently, the Adrenaline GTS 26 dropped, but we’ve not tested it yet. It’s on the list because we loved the 25 so much. The 25 is currently on sale, so grab it while you can.

Some shoes do not have a sexy reputation. Say “stability shoe” to a certain kind of runner and they’ll look like you just suggested they run their next marathon in Crocs. Stability shoes have a reputation problem, and it’s not entirely undeserved. The stability shoes of the early 2000s were clunky, rigid bricks that treated pronation like a disease to be cured with a slab of hard plastic (looking at you, Saucony Grid Azuras). If you ran through that era, I get why you might have a negative, visceral reaction to the type.

In a recent development, but here’s the thing: Stability shoes got better. Today’s versions are lighter, softer, and not for anything? Cuter. And they are some of the best shoes you can lace up—not just for overpronators, but for anyone whose form gets sloppy when the miles pile up. I’ve known runners who white-knuckle their way through marathon blocks in neutral racers when a little guidance would have saved their knees, their IT bands, and frankly, their sourpusses. Needing support isn’t taking an L. It’s biomechanics.

At its simplest, a stability shoe is designed to limit excess inward rolling of the foot (overpronation) after your foot strikes the ground. A little pronation is normal and even beneficial; it helps distribute the shock of the impact. But when your ankle collapses too far inward with every step, that torque travels up the chain to your shins, knees, and hips, and over hundreds of miles it can screw up not just your stride, but your long-term health.

It has been revealed that neutral shoes let your foot do whatever it wants. Stability shoes help guide your foot into a more correct placement, keeping your body more aligned.

From pounding the pavement to scrutinizing performance in our Shoe Lab, the Runner’s World test editors and wear-testers rigorously tested all of our selections. Our process includes exhaustive market research, analysis of user feedback, and consultations with industry experts. This article was written jointly between our editors Amanda Furrer and Cat Bowen. Bowen tends to pronate, especially when she is tired or in a long training block. She has run in all the shoes on this list with the exception of the Nike Structure Plus.

The Brooks Adrenaline GTS 25 is one of the most consistent stability shoes on the market, and the silver anniversary update makes a strong case for why this franchise has lasted 25 years. The big news is in the stack: Brooks added 3 mm to the forefoot and 1 mm to the heel, bringing it to 37 mm and 27 mm respectively, and dropped the heel-to-toe offset from 12 mm down to 10 mm for the first time in the shoe’s history.

It has been revealed that the upcoming heel bevel is the smoothest the Adrenaline has ever had in the opinion of Bowen, who has put serious miles on this shoe. She also feels as though it’s the most balanced this shoe has ever been, and the most balanced on this list.

In a recent development, “Some stability shoes can be so aggressive that the rails can begin to pinch the lateral sides of the foot during long runs,” she indicates. “The Adrenaline GTS 25 doesn’t do that, and they still have the cushion and push to power your runs.”.

According to recent reports, DNA Loft v3 foam carries over from the 24, but the extra volume makes the ride noticeably softer underfoot, especially at heel strike. Guide rails are still doing their thing on the medial and lateral edges—reactive, not prescriptive, engaging only when your stride asks for it. The upper is a breathable engineered mesh that has the benefit of preventing overheating and swamp foot with a stretch knit heel collar that locks down without overcrowding.

Though it should be noted that some testers, including Courtney Kazmierczak, feel as though the collar is a hair too high in the back, which requires some trial and error for sock choice.

In a recent development, at 10.6 ounces, it’s not light, but it’s not trying to be. This is a daily trainer for runners who want structure and protection. It’s a shoe that simply does not pinch or bite.

Shop Men’s at amazon.com | Shop Women’s at amazon.com.

Brooks Adrenaline GTS 25 Review.

This is not a rebuild or huge design change. This is a fine-tuning. The basics are the same; the Adrenaline GTS 26 still uses guide rails as the support system, it has the same stack height, the same drop, the profile hasn’t changed, and the core of the midsole is still the DNA Loft v3 foam.

What did change is that they made it a little bit more breathable by using an engineered mesh upper. The tongue is a bit flatter for a more tuned-in fit, and the heel collar is more refined with a generous pull-tab, which is great for runners with accessibility or limb differences.

Industry observers note that the trade-off here is that it is a teensy bit heavier. We’re talking a few tenths of an ounce difference. And, if I’m being the picky and petty editor that I am? I think the colors and design for this model aren’t as cute. I know, I know, lame thing to bring up, but I really just want a stability shoe in a fun neon. Just because I run like a duck doesn’t mean I don’t deserve fun.

Shop Men’s at brooksrunning.com | Shop Women’s at brooksrunning.com.

Recent findings suggest that these may be our best value pick, but they’re also some of the most durable daily stability trainers on this list. “I like the durability and stability of these shoes and the fact that they are lighter than previous models,” stated shoe tester Lauren Woodall. “I am able to put more miles on these shoes before they need to be replaced than other running shoes.”.

Sources indicate that the thing is, even though it’s heavier, and the durability is noticeable, they’re not bricks. They are your easy run shoes, your throw-on-and-go trainers. They’re not the fastest, but they’re not meant to be. When your body is tired, and you need the assistance of that wave plate and the heft of the Enerzy NXT foam, it’s there for you like an old friend holding out a hand. The guardrails on this shoe aren’t superpowered corrections like they were on earlier models, but the gentle effectiveness of them cannot be overstated. Simply put, these shoes just feel really good on your run.

One note about fit: a few of our testers found that you can get a bit of heel slippage in these. However, Mizuno gives you that extra eyelet for a heel lock, and that can absolutely change the fit of the shoe once you lace up. It’s a point worth remembering.

Shop Men’s at usa.mizuno.com | Shop Women’s at usa.mizuno.com.

The Arahi 9 is Hoka-soft, but not max-cush beefy. It’s a versatile model that does double duty as an everyday trainer or tempo shoe. The brand made small tweaks to the upper for a better fit, and made them a little bit less expensive as well. It’s not a huge redesign as much as it’s a refinement.

You forget the Arahi 9 is a stability shoe because of how streamlined the design looks: it’s sleek and a compliment magnet. Hoka modified the upper to dial in the fit a bit more, make it a little more breathable, and adjust some of the hot points felt in the 8.

It has been revealed that invisible to the eye is the H-Frame system that keeps you stable. The H-Frame is a dense piece of foam in the midsole that’s H-shaped. The result is surprising; you’d think the H-Frame would make the Arahi rigid and heavy, but instead the shoe is lightweight and the ride is smooth. Running in it, Furrer felt like she was gliding.

Shop Men’s at hoka.com | Shop Women’s at hoka.com.

Recent findings suggest that there’s something about the Nike Structure Plus that demands attention. In the words of Furrer, “I have a soft spot for this shoe, it’s just so good on long runs.” And that right there is spot on. For the days when you know you have a long run on the calendar, but that long run is full of mixed tempos, hill climbs, potential obstacles, and rough surfaces that you’ll start to feel underfoot after six miles, this is going to be the shoe you reach for. That’s what Nike designed it to handle when it combined the ReactX and ZoomX foams with a dual-zone rubber outsole. It gives you cushion where you need it, flexibility where it matters most, and a nimble feel when you’re dodging pavement cracks.

Arguably the most stylish shoe on this list, Nike really leveled up its stability line with the Structure. It’s also very orthotic-friendly. The collar and the lacing system can handle a lot of pulling, allowing you to get those insoles in correctly. Beyond that, it’s remarkably comfortable as a shoe just to take out and live in. It’s a solid walking shoe, and we love it as a versatile, more cushioned alternative to wear with dressier outfits.

It has been revealed that that’s not to say it’s flawless. It’s a bit on the heavier side, and if you’re someone who prefers a shoe that has a lot of responsiveness or bounce, you won’t find it in this shoe. It’s also just a hair on the “runs smaller” side front to back. But other than those small quibbles, it’s a great pair.

Shop Men’s at nike.com | Shop Women’s at nike.com.

Sources indicate that the differences between the Gel-Kayano 32 and the 33 are vital, but not massive. They retooled the design of the support system, employing their FluidSupport tech, which is a bit more malleable than previous iterations, working more with the body’s movements and mechanics. They’ve also softened the foam, updated the fit throughout, and for many runners, it should feel and ride more comfortably.

Recent findings suggest that that being remarked, it still has all the Asics features you expect and love: a breathable upper, geometry that works to move you forward, and a grippy sole that keeps you upright on wet pavement. It is on the heavier side, but nothing out of the ordinary for a stability shoe, and the collar could have a hair more cushion. However, we love the well-placed heel tab, especially when our hands are sweaty.

The cushion is going to be the biggest win on long-run days. You may not get a ton of energy return, but what you are getting is that added comfort with the guidance that will help you maintain your form and keep you from hating yourself after the run when you’re inevitably lying on the floor propped up on your hands.

Shop Men’s at asics.com |Shop Women’s at asics.com.

It has been revealed that the Saucony Guide 19 is a stability shoe that actually earns the word “versatile,” which stability shoes rarely do. Most of them feel like you’re being guided rather than running, but the Guide 19 threads the needle between structured support and genuine responsiveness.

The foundation is Pwrrun foam, which delivers a cushioned but not marshmallow-soft ride. It’s lively enough to handle tempo work without feeling like you’re fighting the shoe, and cushioned enough that you’re not destroyed after 18 miles. The medial TPU guidance frame offers mild overpronation correction without the brick-like rigidity you get from old-school posts. It’s more a gentle steer rather than having the shoe take the reins and navigate your feet for you.

Recent findings suggest that for long runs, the 8 mm drop and 32 mm stack height in the heel keep things comfortable for time-on-feet without creating that spongy instability that kills your form late in a run. For daily training, it’s durable and consistent and a shoe you can lace up without thinking too hard about what’s on your schedule.

In a recent development, and it’s just plain comfortable. At least according to our wear-tester Dave Block, who “can’t remember a shoe that’s felt this great.” And even for tempo days on the track, the fit on this shoe just gets it right. It fits snugly enough that at faster paces it doesn’t feel sloppy.It won’t replace a racing flat, but for runners who want one shoe that handles most of their weekly mileage without drama, the Guide 19 makes a strong case.

Shop Men’s at saucony.com |Shop Women’s at saucony.com.

What separates the Hoka Rocket X 3 from other super shoes is its broader base and accommodating fit. The shoe has a winged carbon plate to help with propulsion and a dual-density PEBA midsole to provide high energy return and supportive cushioning. An notable enhancement: a sticky rubber outsole to prevent slipping and sliding when the race forecast predicts rain or snow.

“These shoes were very stable, which is different for a racing shoe,” indicates tester Shane Houghton, an overpronator. “Most super shoes feel kind wobbly but I felt lower to the ground and never felt in danger of rolling an ankle. When I stand in the shoes I feel flat on my feet and I don’t feel any lateral-rocking. I had no anxiety wearing these during loopy intervals or running around curves. The lacing is tight and like the texture of the ribbed laces. It keeps them from coming undone or loosening while running.”.

Sometimes, shoes that are very much stabilizing or stability-adjacent shirk that term for optics. I can’t prove it, but I believe the Nike ACG Zegamas fit that description.

I’ve spent months running in these, and as someone who pronates frequently, I can tell you they deliver the structure and support of a true stability shoe wrapped in the rugged outsole of a trail runner. It comes down to that revised last. The Zegama cups the outer rim of your foot so thoroughly that it holds you locked in place, correcting the roll before it starts.

Sources indicate that the support straps built into the upper wrap all the way around your foot, the padded tongue and lacing lock your midfoot down, and the heel keeps you planted without any slip. It doesn’t feel neutral, but it doesn’t steer you, either. Instead, it almost feels like it’s anticipatory rather than corrective.

Pair that underfoot security with a grippy Vibram outsole and aggressive lugs that bite into mud and wet rock, and you get the best of both worlds—the stable, planted feel of a stability shoe with the traction to handle whatever the trail throws at you.

Shop Men’s at nike.com | Shop Women’s at nike.com.

With any piece of running equipment, comfort should be your foremost deciding factor. Here are a few thing to consider before your next shoe fitting:.

1) The shoe should have enough room for your toes to splay in the toebox, about a thumbnail’s width from the front of the shoe to the tip of your longest toe.

2) The shoe shouldn’t feel too tight or loose around the midfoot area. There are lacing techniques to help modify your shoe’s width, but you should also consider different widths instead of the standard D (men) or B (women) width.

Sources indicate that 3) A secure heel is also paramount, as slippage can cause blisters. The heel-lock lacing method—threading each lace in the etra eyelet next to it to create a loop, then crisscrossing the opposite laces through the loop to create a “lock”—can give you a more secure fit.

4) Give the shoes a run at the store or check website’s return/exchange policies. Besides trying on the shoe, the best way to know if it’s comfy is if you run in it, too.

In a recent development, some runners want maximum cushioning underfoot while others want less padding to experience more ground feel. New foam technology has given us the best of both worlds with plush, high-stacked cushioning that’s lightweight, too. Because of these high stack heights, stability tech is added to help runners run course tangents—and not twist their ankles while doing so.

Industry observers note that still, shoes with thicker cushioning and a high stack (36mm or more) tend to be squishier, making them less stable. Shoes with lower stack heights (32mm or less in the heel) provide a closer-to-the-ground feel and better feedback.

According to recent reports, you don’t have to give up max-cushioning if you’re an overpronator, however. Besides looking for shoes with built-in stability features, like guide rails and stability planes, consider shoes with wide, exaggerated soles, particularly under the heel, and a wider midfoot. Raised sidewalls (the interior padded sides of the shoe) create a snugger fit that will also enhance support, ensuring optimal stability and comfort.

Besides looking for shoes with stability features, you should also consider the type of workouts you’ll be performing in these shoes.

It has been revealed that for speedwork, like tempos and track workouts, lightweight trainers (less than 9 ounces for men or 8 ounces for women) with a curved “rocker” midsole help you surge forward. For everyday runs and longer runs, slightly heavier shoes with more padding provide the comfort and durability that you want on a daily training run. Or if you’re interested in venturing off-road, it’s key to have a trail shoe made for rough, undulating terrain.

Do I actually need a stability shoe?

Stability shoes are specifically designed for overpronation, a type of gait pattern when your foot rolls too far inward upon landing. Flat-foot, low arch runners can also benefit from this extra padding in shoes.

Sources indicate that not every flat-foot runner or overpronator may need the extra support, however, especially if their feet only have a slight roll. We strongly advise having your gait evaluated by a professional, such as a podiatrist, physical therapist, or movement specialist. They can confirm if you need motion-specific shoes or an orthotic insert.

The best stability shoes focus on enhancing comfort and promoting a natural gait rather than imposing a harsh, corrective feel. While extra padding may sound like a plus, it can be too prescriptive for some runners. Worst-case scenario: Overcorrecting a neutral stride could increase your chance of injury, rather than make you more comfortable.

If you’re a upcoming runner unsure of your gait pattern, we recommend running in a neutral shoe, like the Hoka Clifton 11s, first.

When should neutral runners consider wearing a stability shoe?

Some shoes with stability tech lend support to late-onset overpronators, i.e., neutral runners whose form becomes erratic midrun due to fatigue. Brands like Brooks and Altra, for instance, use denser foam on the medial and lateral sides of the midsole to help control excessive movement and promote knee and foot alignment, resulting in a more efficient stride.

Is there an adjustment to running in stability shoes?

It has been revealed that as with any running shoe transition, like trying zero-drop trainers for the first time, you’ll want to gradually make the switch if you usually wear neutral shoes. Start with shorter runs and then slowly ramp up mileage or runtime as your body adjusts to the new shoes. Read your body for cues; if you feel some discomfort you may need a slower process before fully committing to stability shoes. Muscle fatigue and pain can also be non-shoe-related and be attributed to overuse. If this is not the glitch and it is the shoes, discontinue running in them and talk to a specialist for further evaluation.

Do stability shoes “fix” overpronation?

Recent findings suggest that no. Instead, they support your existing gait pattern. Your shoes can make you feel more comfortable and stable, but it doesn’t change that pattern.

In the words of Test Editor Morgan Petruny: “Keep in mind that a stability shoe is not a cure-all or magic pill. Rather, it is a tool.”.

Overpronation can be due to various factors, including biomechanics, muscle strength, and flexibility, so stability shoes are just one component of a comprehensive approach to managing its negative effects. Strengthening exercises, gait analysis, and proper running form can also play vital roles in that effort.

According to recent reports, cat Bowen, senior editor of commerce; reviews, is a seasoned runner with more than 20 years of distance running experience, including dozens of marathons, half marathons, and even a few ultra marathons. For over a decade, she has tested parenting, fitness, home, and running gear and written in-depth guides to help readers with their next purchase. Holding multiple advanced degrees and currently studying kinesiology, Cat Bowen brings research-backed insight to all of her guides. Passionate about women’s health and neurodivergent inclusion, she advocates for closing research gaps and helping others—especially AudHD people—find joy in running and fitness.

She has reviewed gear and covered other topics in the running space for almost 10 years. Since 2013, she has consecutively run the Boston Marathon. She also has a master’s degree in gastronomy from Boston University and was formerly a professional baker for two years before hanging up her apron.

Tech Report: ‘One of a Million’: She’s 3-Foot-9, Just Ran a 3:42 Marathon, and Is Chasing a Boston Qualifier

💡 Key Takeaways
