  • During a marathon, Juli Windsor admits she doesn’t always get to take in the scenery.
  • It has been revealed that “Most runners can see what's coming ahead, and they can see beyond the shoulders and all the heads,” she said.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

We earn a commission for products purchased through some links in this article. Why Trust Us?

During a marathon, Juli Windsor admits she doesn’t always get to take in the scenery.

It has been revealed that “Most runners can see what's coming ahead, and they can see beyond the shoulders and all the heads,” she said. “For me, my view is hundreds of butts. It’s not the most inspirational view.”.

It’s one difference that Windsor, who is 3-foot-9, has learned to navigate as a runner with dwarfism. But that hasn't stopped her from beating many of those butts in races.

At the Indianapolis Marathon on November 7, Windsor, 39, ran 3:42:00 to finish in the top third of her 35–39 age group, averaging an 8:28 mile pace. The time was a PR by seven minutes and is provisionally a new American record for the T40 para category (a division for athletes with short stature).

Recent findings suggest that windsor was born with an extremely rare form of dwarfism called acromesomelic dysplasia. “Last I heard, I’m one of a million,” stated Windsor, who works as a physician assistant in developmental pediatrics.

Recent findings suggest that windsor’s run in Indianapolis is more impressive considering that this is part two of her marathoning career. After taking a decade off to raise her two kids in 2014, Windsor has come back even stronger, knocking off more than an hour from her pre-hiatus personal best.

Sources indicate that “I just think the human body is just such an amazing thing,” she said. “And that when asked something difficult of it, what you’re capable of doing can sometimes be really surprising.”.

According to recent reports, as a middle schooler, Windsor joined the track team to hang out with her friends and went in with low expectations. But that changed when she beat another runner in an 800-meter race. It was motivating, and Windsor eventually realized that although she couldn’t dust her peers in a sprint, she had exceptional grit and endurance. “I might not be able to outrun them, but I could outlast them,” she remembers.

In her twenties, Windsor set her sights on the marathon—and one marathon in particular. She wanted to become the first person with dwarfism to run the prestigious Boston Marathon. In 2013, her dream almost came true, but as she neared the finish line on Boylston Street, she was forced to stop. Terrorists had detonated bombs at the finish. Windsor was unharmed, but her dream would have to wait.

The next year, Windsor became the first person with dwarfism to complete the historic race, running 4:43:26. That would be her last marathon for a decade, as Windsor raised two kids and focused on her family.

According to recent reports, in 2025, she felt pulled back to the distance. She signed up for the Spinx Marathon in Greenville, South Carolina, where she ran 4:09:51—more than 30 minutes faster than her personal best from Boston.

Industry observers note that not long after, Windsor started working with coach Esther Atkins, a former professional marathoner who coaches with McKirdy Trained. Atkins saw potential in Windsor and had a hunch she could run a lot faster. While unsure at first, Windsor was assuaged when she nabbed another massive personal best, running 3:49:42 at the 2026 Boston Marathon in April.

Atkins, who works with about 40 athletes, is impressed by how coachable Windsor is. “She’s always open to trying something different, and very eager to push the boundaries of what she has done before or what she has believed she was capable of,” Atkins mentioned.

“I’m not used to people expecting more of me than I expect of myself; usually it’s the other way around,” Windsor said. “And that’s how I know I have an exceptional coach. She sees the possibilities and isn’t stumped by my unique challenges.”.

As a runner with dwarfism, Windsor is presented with obstacles that most runners don’t face. Her cadence, for example, is much higher than the average runner. While 180 steps per minute is a commonly cited target among runners, Windsor averaged 207 steps per minute at Indianapolis, and because her stride length is much shorter, she covers less ground per step. (For reference, Windsor is about the height of an average 6-year-old.).

In a recent development, windsor also has to navigate crowds carefully—she doesn’t always show up in the peripheral vision of competitors. She generally runs on the right side of the road to improve her visibility and avoid getting tripped up or surprising people as she passes. At larger races, like Boston or Indy, she is able to start a few minutes ahead of the masses to let the race string out.

In a recent development, and then there are shoes. Windsor wears a kids’ size 13, but it’s hard to find athletic shoes in her size that aren’t Velcro or light-up. She generally sizes up to a size 1 for running shoes and uses custom orthotics. But such small sizes don’t have the bells and whistles of normal running shoes. And super shoes that small don’t exist.

Recent findings suggest that so far, Windsor has liked Asics the best. “I don’t think I fully appreciated the difference of having a good quality shoe until I tried [an Asics shoe] on,” she stated. “And even just having a gel cushion was like, ‘Is this how everybody else feels? This is what I've been missing out on.’”.

Recent findings suggest that windsor ran Indianapolis in the GT-2000, although they’re still a little pared down compared to a mass-market adult shoe. “I really wish there were better options and better technology, because I've had to just work with what my options are,” she said.

According to recent reports, until recently, Windsor wasn’t able to find a GPS watch that fit her wrists. Last summer, she discovered that Garmin made a 42mm watch, which finally allowed her to run without a phone and gave her insights like cadence and stride length. She partially credits the data for her recent improvement.

According to recent reports, looking ahead, Windsor has two goals. The first is to qualify for Boston in her age group. Windsor has already nabbed a BQ in the adaptive athlete field, but she’s targeting the able-bodied BQ. She turns 40 next spring, which will bump her to the 40–44 age group. She’ll need to run under 3:35:00—about 7 minutes faster than her personal best—to achieve the standard.

Her other goal is to create more opportunities for runners in her Paralympic category. Presently, World ParaAthletics doesn’t sanction running events in the short stature division. USATF recently began to include the marathon in the T40 category, a record which Windsor owns. But the record book isn’t what drives her.

Industry observers note that “It's less about competition, more about just setting some sort of a standard, and that records are meant to be broken …” she mentioned. “I would love for to open up opportunities for people to at least be curious and give it a try.”.

According to recent reports, next up for Windsor? The Tokyo Marathon on March 7—one week before her 40th birthday.

Industry observers note that theo Kahler is the senior news editor at Runner’s World. He’s a former all-conference collegiate runner at Winthrop University, and he received his master’s degree in liberal arts studies from Wake Forest University, where he was a member of one of the top distance-running teams in the NCAA. Kahler has reported on the ground at major events such as the Paris Olympics, U.S. Olympic Trials, New York City Marathon, and Boston Marathon. He’s run 14:20 in the 5K, 1:05:37 in the half marathon, and finished 40th at the 2025 New York City Marathon. He enjoys spotting tracks from the sky on airplanes. (Look for colorful ovals around football fields.).

#126553. The Benefits of Biking for Seniors, Including the Mental and Physical Payoffs

The Benefits of Biking for Seniors, Including the Mental and Physical Payoffs

📅 09 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 10 min read (2082 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Bicycling

⏱️ ~10 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review.
  • We know you think we’re going to tell you all the ways cycling improves your heart health and muscle strength—and it does, but guess what?
  • In fact, even though many people associate aging with physical and mental declines, regular exercise—like a daily bike ride—can help slow or even reverse some of these effects.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review. We may earn commission if you buy from a link. How we test gear.

We know you think we’re going to tell you all the ways cycling improves your heart health and muscle strength—and it does, but guess what? According to a 2023 scoping review in Frontiers in Sports and Active Living, studies show that when older adults cycle regularly, their happiness improves and they are better able to maintain their quality of life.

In fact, even though many people associate aging with physical and mental declines, regular exercise—like a daily bike ride—can help slow or even reverse some of these effects.

Read More of Ride Strong at 50+.

Industry observers note that “Regular physical activity helps seniors maintain good health, improve their quality of life, and increase their overall well-being,” Mary Sabat, MS, RDN, a personal trainer and dietitian in Georgia tells Bicycling. “It can enhance physical strength, flexibility, and endurance, making it easier to perform daily activities and maintain independence.”.

Those are just few reasons why biking for seniors is so great—but here are all the advantages you gain when you start pedaling regularly.

Recent findings suggest that while almost forms of physical activity improve physical and mental health, cycling is particularly well-suited for those in their golden years due to its accessibility. After all, cycling is easy on the joints, even for those with joint pain or injuries. “It can be tailored to individual fitness levels and adjusted to accommodate different abilities and physical limitations, too,” claims Sabat. “Recumbent bikes, trikes, or electric-assist bicycles can be used to make cycling more accessible for those with mobility challenges or balance challenges.”.

Sources indicate that robert Patterson, a cyclist and lawyer, has been cycling for more than 40 years. He points out all the obvious aerobic and strength-building gains he’s enjoyed over the years, but also the psychological benefits. “Cycling also benefits my mental health. My attitude and overall focus are always improved by being on the bike,” he says.

Here are nine reasons, according to the experts, for you to saddle up and hit the road (or the gym) for a ride.

Aerobic exercise is the key to managing heart health. Because the heart is a muscle, it needs to be exercised on a regular basis to maintain its strength and optimal function. And because the heart and lungs work together with the venous system to deliver oxygenated blood to your muscles, any exercise that increases your heart rate and breath rate for an extended period of time will help improve your heart health and overall cardiovascular function.

According to recent reports, plus, as anyone who has ever pushed the pedals and pumped through a 20- or 30-minute bike ride knows, cycling will definitely get your heart rate up. The repetitive cycling motion qualifies as a moderate to intense form of aerobic exercise that you can easily adapt to your personal fitness level. This means that even if you haven’t exercised in years, by starting at a lower intensity and making adjustments to your workouts based on your heart rate, you can safely and effectively add cycling to your weekly routine.

“As individuals age, the risk of heart disease increases,” says Sabat. “Cycling is a low-impact aerobic exercise that helps improve cardiovascular fitness, strengthens the heart muscle, and enhances blood circulation. It can lower the risk of heart attacks, strokes, and high blood pressure, thereby promoting a healthy heart.”.

In fact, a series of two 2019 review studies (part 1 and part 2) published in the British Journal of Sports Medicine found that all forms of cycling reduce the risk of cardiovascular disease and also reduced the risk factor profile for poor heart health—meaning that cyclists had better body composition stats, blood lipid profiles, cardiorespiratory fitness levels, and more time spent exercising. All of these together help mitigate the risk for developing heart disease.

In a recent development, you can combat practically any chronic condition, including heart disease, along with type 2 diabetes, arthritis, and cancer with a regular ride. Exercise helps keep the blood flowing, systems moving, and cells turning over in a way that promotes overall health. For instance, high-intensity exercise (and high-intensity cycling, specifically) helps improve blood glucose response, according to research, which may reduce the risk of type 2 diabetes.

It has been revealed that even in the case of cancer, participating in a regular cycling routine has been shown to reduce the risk. For example, May 2020 study published in The Lancet found an association between participating in a daily bike commute and a 16 percent decrease in cancer mortality and an 11 percent decrease in cancer incidence.

“By incorporating a ride here and there into their routine, seniors can reduce the risk of chronic conditions. These conditions can be debilitating, but with regular exercise, seniors can take proactive steps toward prevention and management,” Josh Weight, a certified sports physiotherapist and the director of Gravity Physio in Australia tells Bicycling.

Industry observers note that it’s not unusual for seniors to experience regular joint pain associated with arthritis or previous injuries. In fact, according to the National Poll on Healthy Aging, about 70 percent of older adults report current joint pain. This can be exacerbated by extended periods spent sitting, or simply not moving around much, as sedentary behavior is directly associated with increased incidences of knee and other joint pain.

While on the surface this may not seem like a substantial deal, it can lead to a cascading series of events where joint pain or arthritis contributes to a reduced range of motion. This reduced range of motion can influence balance, coordination, and even the ability to perform everyday tasks. These challenges can also contribute to a reduced quality of life and even an increased risk of falls. As such, any activity that can be done without contributing to joint pain while protecting and strengthening the structures that help stabilize the joints (muscles, tendons, and ligaments) is an key undertaking for older adults’ overall health and well-being.

It has been revealed that “Cycling is a low-impact activity that puts minimal stress on the joints, making it an excellent option for individuals with joint-related issues. It provides a cardiovascular workout without placing excessive strain on the knees, hips, or ankles,” Sabat indicates.

According to recent reports, whether done on an indoor bike or a more traditional road or mountain bike, one thing’s for sure: Cycling works the legs. It takes muscular strength, power, and endurance to keep the pedals moving, especially when climbing a hill or ramping up the resistance. But it’s not just the legs and glutes that benefit—cycling can help build strength in the shoulders, upper back, and core, as well.

Of course, you may not be looking to build massive quads as one of your long-term fitness goals, but developing muscular strength isn’t just about looking strong—it’s about maintaining your quality of life.

According to recent reports, research estimates muscle mass begins to decline by 3 to 8 percent every decade following your 30th birthday, with those rates increasing further once you hit 60. This age-related muscular decline over time makes it more challenging to continue doing everyday activities like climbing stairs or carrying groceries. It’s crucial to participate in exercises, like cycling, that will help maintain or build muscle mass over time to safeguard your ability to perform these daily activities.

It has been revealed that in fact, according to a 2015 review study published in the European Review of Aging and Physical Activity, adults over 70 years of age experienced increased muscular strength and power when participating in a cycling exercise program at least three times a week for 12 to 16 weeks. This data flies in the face of anyone who believes they can’t develop muscle or strength as they age—it’s not only possible, it’s critical to overall health and functional ability.

One area in which cycling can be particularly beneficial is balance and coordination. This has ties to muscular strength, as strong, trained muscles tend to perform and react more promptly to stimuli than those that aren’t worked regularly. However, it also has to do with the unique requirements of cycling itself.

“Cycling requires balance and coordination to stay upright and navigate,” says Andrew White, a personal trainer and owner of Garage Gym Pro. “This can be especially beneficial for seniors as these abilities tend to decline with age, increasing the risk of falls and injuries.”.

This isn’t just conjecture—a 2018 prospective study published in the Journal of Aging and Physical Activity found that older adults (between the ages of 65 and 85) who cycled daily had better balance, a faster pace while walking, and better self-reported lower-extremity function compared to those who didn’t bike regularly. Based on this study, it appears that cycling helps preserve balance and coordination which contributes to lower-body function that can help prevent falls.

Just as muscle mass tends to decline with age, an associated change in body composition takes place, which often leads to increased weight gain. And as weight creeps up, so do the risks for heart disease and chronic illness, particularly in populations considered obese.

Recent findings suggest that cycling and other forms of exercise can help keep weight and other disease risk factors in check. This is partly due to the muscle-protective benefits exercise offers, but also due to the increased calorie burn that occurs during moderate- to high-intensity exercise like cycling.

“Cycling can help seniors maintain a healthy body weight, reduce excess body fat, and prevent obesity-related health problems,” Sabat emphasizes.

It’s not unusual for seniors to experience social isolation that can contribute to physical and mental health decline. Changes in health, mobility, or driving status can keep seniors alone at home. This is unfortunate because strong social connections are positively associated with longevity.

It has been revealed that cycling can provide seniors with an accessible way to get out and about, and to also engage with other people of all ages. “Cycling can be an enjoyable and social activity for seniors. Exploring outdoor trails, participating in group rides, or engaging in community cycling events can foster a sense of camaraderie and connection with others,” indicates Weight.

And for seniors who want to start cycling, but don’t know how, community cycling clubs offer a great way to learn and connect at the same time.

According to recent reports, in addition to the benefits of social interaction, cycling can boost mental health in a number of ways, especially if you’re riding your bike outside. “Cycling outdoors provides an opportunity to connect with nature, which can be therapeutic and stress-relieving,” says White.

According to recent reports, in fact, according to a 2022 study published in the Journal of Affective Disorders, individuals who participated in outdoor cycling (or other outdoor activities like walking, jogging, or team sports), were less likely to experience depression than those who were inactive. Likewise, there’s evidence that even a single outdoor exercise session (like cycling) can impact mood, more than indoor exercise equivalents.

In a recent development, even in the absence of an outdoor setting, physical activity as a whole is good for mental health. “Regular exercise releases endorphins which can elevate mood and reduce symptoms of anxiety and depression,” Sabat explains.

One final benefit of cycling for seniors: It can support cognitive function. “Studies have shown that physical activity can have positive effects on cognition and may help reduce the risk of cognitive decline and dementia in older adults. Exercise promotes better blood flow to the brain, stimulates the release of hormones that support brain health, and improves memory and attention,” Sabat shares.

Laura Williams, M.S., ACSM EP-C holds a master's degree in exercise and sport science and is a certified exercise physiologist through the American College of Sports Medicine. She also holds sports nutritionist, youth fitness, sports conditioning, and behavioral change specialist certifications through the American Council on Exercise. She has been writing on health, fitness, and wellness for 12 years, with bylines appearing online and in print for Men's Health, Healthline, Verywell Fit, The Healthy, Giddy, Thrillist, Men's Journal, Reader's Digest, and Runner's World. After losing her first husband to cancer in 2018, she moved to Costa Rica to use surfing, beach running, and horseback riding as part of her healing process. There, she met her current husband, had her son, and now splits time between Texas and Costa Rica.

#126552. Latest Update: After 50 Years of Running, I’m Facing My Toughest Challenge: Having to Let Go of the Runner I Used to Be

📅 17 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 8m • 📚 Deep Dive (1528 w)

Latest Update: After 50 Years of Running, I’m Facing My Toughest Challenge: Having to Let Go of the Runner I Used to Be

📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1528 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Runnersworld

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, “Some runs are shouts, and some runs are whispers,” I wrote a few decades back in Runner’s World Complete Book of Women’s Running, an attempt to capture the many moods—the many functions—that running served in my life.
  • Industry observers note that I chuckled a little upon seeing it.
  • This latest reality that came with illness and settled in for the long haul wasn’t easy to accept.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, “Some runs are shouts, and some runs are whispers,” I wrote a few decades back in Runner’s World Complete Book of Women’s Running, an attempt to capture the many moods—the many functions—that running served in my life. I scrolled past the phrase recently on social media: Somebody had designed it with colors and typography and posted it, apparently finding resonance in the sentiment.

Industry observers note that I chuckled a little upon seeing it. If I wrote that today, I’d add something else: “Some runs are walks.”.

This latest reality that came with illness and settled in for the long haul wasn’t easy to accept. I’ve been running on and off for more than 50 years, some 85 percent of my life. I jogged along with my older brother when I was a girl, competed in high school as a teen, trained for a sub-3 marathon as a working professional in my 30s, plodded with a baby jogger in my 40s. Now, past 60, running has shape-shifted again. The transformation is different this time, the lessons deeper and, frankly, a little harder to grasp. But after a period of struggle, I’ve made peace with it. Because as usual, if you dare to listen, running will speak to you.

Sources indicate that most of us who run spend years or even decades seeking to improve, from a 5K to 10K, from breaking 4 hours in a marathon to then trying for 3:45. For a long time, wherever you are, improvement is possible, and change generally trends in one direction. Not every run, of course. The body has good days and challenging ones; that variability is a given, and progress is not a straight line. But we can expect a trajectory that provides a satisfactory feedback loop, one of betterment.

Sources indicate that inevitably, aging will bend the line of progression into an arc. We can know that and still have trouble seeing it at first, because the heavy legs or knee catching feels like just another hard day. Nothing a little rest or cross-training can’t solve.

Industry observers note that if seeing it is difficult, accepting it can be even harder. The forward march has been the natural state of things for so long. The battle waged for incremental increases in mileage or decreases in time was never easy. Shouldn’t I be pushing past this? Isn’t it what runners do?

Running taught me to be tough. For years, that served me even beyond the sport. In work, the tug of fatigue from long nights at the ad agency felt familiar and manageable as a long run. Giving birth called back the discipline of breathing through pain; the years of motherhood to come called in the lessons of patience, of quietly putting in the hours without immediate affirmation or result. I loved being a badass in the endurance sport of life. The ability to override tiredness felt powerful. I enjoyed telling myself I was fine when evidence pointed to the contrary. I relished pushing against edges and limits.

According to recent reports, until the day I woke, swung my feet over the side of the bed to stand, and felt the world spin wildly out of control. The floor rushed up to my face, and I curled in a ball seeking safety and stillness. Confusion mingled with nausea. I could feel the whirling even with eyes closed. The fetal position proved fitting. I’d spend years relearning how to be in this new world, where vertigo could strike at any time.

My first reaction was “I’ll fight!” Though for months that thought came while I was sprawled on the couch, unable to focus my eyes or lift my arms. A year of doctor visits, scans, and tests eventually ruled out physical problems and delivered a neurological diagnosis: vestibular migraine. As with other forms of migraine, the condition is underdiagnosed, women suffer more than men, and precious little is understood about what is actually happening in the brain to produce the symptoms. Some connection has been made to hormonal fluctuations, and, for some, a genetic link seems to exist; stress, I learned, is a reliable exacerbator of triggers.

My own onset remains a mystery.

The impulse to fight landed ineffectually in space against the judo of forced rest. Any struggle against this opponent would only feed it. Somewhere along the way, a latest understanding dawned: Vertigo was my body saying, “Stop.”.

According to recent reports, tough got me here, but it wasn’t going to get me through this next chapter. The fighting stance I’d adopted so long ago was not going to serve me well with the changes happening now. Some things about the body are not in our control, despite our best efforts. With precious few alternatives, I did something I never had before: I paused, I listened to what my body was saying, and I opened to the possibility of unlearning some things that running and life had drilled into me so very long ago. This time the lesson wasn’t about pushing through. It’s also not a sob story about slowing down. It is about acceptance.

Now, three years since my first vertigo attack, something akin to gratitude has set in. The softening and adapting are treasured new tools. Essential new tools. Because the fact is: you don’t “overcome” aging.

Sources indicate that nowadays, when I’m feeling good enough to put on my shorts and running shoes, I might have an idea of what I’d like to do. But it’s just that, an idea. I start slowly, so as not to tweak a knee or an ankle. Eventually, my body will tell me what this day has in store. If I’m lightheaded and the sun feels too bright, triggering aural distortion, I walk and think, yes, it is a fine day for a walk. If I feel strong, I push to the degree I can and think, how wonderful, to feel good. Neither situation really surprises me anymore. None of it is bad. I feel lucky to be out here.

In a recent development, the point is this: It is all like this now. And if I can’t accept that in my running, I’m going to be in for an exhausting battle with every other part of aging. Don’t mistake this for giving up. I am working harder to stay fit than I have in a very long time. Pushing the pace all those years? It came pretty easy. It felt damned good. What I’m doing now takes more effort: Spin classes that give my knees a break... and where 80-year-olds are dusting me. Full-body lifting that leaves every hidden muscle protesting. Yoga classes that make it clear balance has never been a prerequisite for anything before in my life. The objective now isn’t performance—it’s simply to age as well as possible.

Sources indicate that there is no fairness in this, no way that this “should” go. Aging comes differently for us all, as an entire generation who grew up during the first running boom is now learning. Our running will change in its own way, a reflection of everything we have done before, plus the ineffable element of luck.

Recent findings suggest that my son-in-law’s mother is one of those seemingly defying the years. Pushing 60, she’s also pushing into fresh territory with a string of 50K trail races. Her streak of runs is proudly documented on Strava, which cheerily alerts me every time she becomes the “Local Legend” of some new stretch.

She’s excited, posting every day, a wide smile spread across her face. She exudes the joy of progress. I’m a bit envious, sure. I’m also glad for her. Both things can be true.

It has been revealed that I have other friends who do not run anymore. In one way or another, their bodies—joints that didn’t respond to surgery, chronic illness that has sapped their energy—have let them know those days are done. The ones doing the best move on, find new challenges.

My joy comes from somewhere else now. It’s not so much the running per se; rather, everything around it. The feeling of autumn’s first cool air on my shoulders. The smell of spring’s thawing mud. The sheer pleasure of moving through space outdoors one more day. In fact, these things are more present than before, without the distraction of pace and goals.

If my running taught me everything about how to persist, why wouldn’t it be the thing to teach me about how to let go? Our running is always “becoming.” Just as we are ourselves. We have an opportunity to learn from it, because the fact is that running isn’t the only thing that is changing.

As with everything else, it might not be the lesson you want, but it’s always the lesson you need.

It has been revealed that dagny Scott is the author of Runner’s World Complete Book of Women’s Running. She is at the moment working on a book that explores the beauty in finding authenticity and acceptance in an aging body. Scott lives, writes, runs, and walks in Boulder, Colorado.

#126550. Are Your Recovery Runs Too Long? Experts Explain the Line Between Productive Recovery and Added Fatigue

📅 18 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 7m • 📚 Deep Dive (1361 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Runnersworld ↗ Open Full Page

Are Your Recovery Runs Too Long? Experts Explain the Line Between Productive Recovery and Added Fatigue

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1361 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Runnersworld

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that we earn a commission for products purchased through some links in this article.
  • Recent findings suggest that getting faster isn’t just about training harder.
  • While there’s plenty of advice about the importance of rest days and how slowly you should go during easy recovery runs, there’s considerably less discussion about exactly how long those runs should last.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that we earn a commission for products purchased through some links in this article. Why Trust Us?

Recent findings suggest that getting faster isn’t just about training harder. It also requires smarter recovery.

While there’s plenty of advice about the importance of rest days and how slowly you should go during easy recovery runs, there’s considerably less discussion about exactly how long those runs should last.

According to recent reports, major picture, recovery runs should help you stay consistent between harder sessions; they shouldn’t leave you carrying extra fatigue into your next workout. However, simply running at an easy pace doesn’t guarantee an easy training load because the longer you run, the more energy you use and the more repetitive impact you take on.

So how long should your recovery runs last to maintain the volume-building, bloodflow-boosting benefits? And what signs mean it’s time to cut the run short?

We asked run coaches and exercise physiologists to explain how to find the right recovery run duration to ensure you’re not dragging for your next workout and when calling it a (rest) day might work best.

In a recent development, recovery runs allow runners to increase their overall aerobic training volume without taking a complete rest day after every hard session, notes run coach, author, and founder of 80/20 Endurance, Matt Fitzgerald. For instance, if the sole objective were to recover from quality runs as quickly as possible, total rest (a.k.a. not running at all) is more effective.

But receiving the benefits of recovery runs without elevating fatigue or injury risk depends on keeping duration within a certain range.

Sources indicate that “As a run extends, we’re also continuing to consume energy and introduce mechanical load,” explains Pamela Geisel, CSCS, RRCA-certified run coach, exercise physiologist, and director of Performance and Wellness Services at the Hospital for Special Surgery in New York City. In other words, your muscles are still contracting, your body is still using fuel, and your bones, tendons, and joints are absorbing the repetitive impact of every stride.

If you extend a recovery run too long, the stress caused by this additional workload begins to outweigh the aerobic benefits of the run and can lead to the aforementioned heightened fatigue and injury risk, especially if you’re recovering from a particularly demanding training session.

It has been revealed that this logic is exactly why experts all agree that recovery runs absolutely can go on for too long. The tricky part is finding the line.

“There’s no established duration or mileage at which an easy run becomes detrimental to recovery,” says Michael Landram, an exercise physiologist and assistant professor at the University of Scranton.

Instead, each person’s ideal duration depends on a variety of factors, including training history, current fatigue, nutrition, sleep, and the demands of any upcoming workouts, Landram explains.

Here’s a three-step checklist for making sure yours fall in the right range.

Usually, Geisel recommends keeping recovery runs between 20 and 40 minutes in length, but that window should shift depending on how much you’re accustomed to running.

Industry observers note that for example, if you’re averaging around 20 miles per week, Geisel suggests aiming for approximately 15 to 25 minutes. If you’re regularly logging up to 60 miles per week, you can pencil in 25- to 45-minute recovery sessions.

It has been revealed that and remember, these recommendations are starting points, not strict limits. Danny Mackey, head coach of the Brooks Beasts Track Club, claims he might prescribe a recovery run of just 20 minutes for an 800-meter specialist, while long-distance runners accustomed to running 75 to 80 miles per week can comfortably handle a 60-minute recovery run.

Additionally, it’s important to take into consideration how long you’ve maintained your current weekly mileage.

Sources indicate that landram explains that a runner who’s consistently logged 50-mile weeks for several years may tolerate longer recovery runs than someone who’s only recently built up to that level. Even if both runners in this example have similar cardiovascular fitness, their muscles may not be equally adapted to the repetitive demands of 50-mile weeks.

So, if you’ve recently increased your weekly mileage, stick to shorter recovery runs and gradually extend their duration as your body adjusts.

If you’re relatively latest to running, are only running a few days per week, or have only easy runs on your schedule as you build endurance and consistency, you may not need a dedicated recovery run at all. Rest days allow for proper rejuvenation between workouts.

Fitzgerald recommends using your typical easy-run duration as a reference point and making recovery runs shorter and slower (zone 1, anyone?). If your scheduled easy runs are usually 60 minutes long, for instance, a recovery run—particularly one scheduled after hard, quality workouts—might last 40 minutes or less, at an even lower intensity.

If you’ve just completed a particularly demanding interval session, long run, or race, consider keeping your recovery run at the shorter end of your usual range. The same applies if you have another hard workout scheduled within the next 24 to 48 hours.

Heat, hills, and uneven terrain can also make an otherwise easy session more taxing, so it’s worth considering an even shorter duration in those circumstances.

Overall, your recovery-run duration should reflect what your body is accustomed to handling, rather than a mileage target you’re trying to reach.

Even if you’ve planned your recovery run carefully, it’s important to pay attention to how your body responds once you start moving.

In a recent development, one of the first warning signs is a change in perceived exertion. If your usual recovery pace suddenly feels harder than it should or your legs feel unusually heavy, you may need to reconsider how long you’re running.

Geisel also recommends paying attention to changes in your stride, including heavier foot strikes and other form challenges getting worse as the run progresses.

The metrics available on your watch can also indicate a recovery run has gone too long. For example, an unusually elevated heart rate at your normal easy pace may signal you’re carrying too much fatigue, Landram explains. Though remember heat, dehydration, sleep, and stress can also affect heart rate, so pair it with how you feel to determine if you’re going too long.

Sources indicate that if you’re feeling unusually tired during a recovery run, Shannon Hugard, a biomechanics researcher at the University of Oregon, recommends a simple midrun check-in. “If you’re feeling more fatigued or sore than usual, run that first mile,” she advises. “See how you’re feeling. If you’re still sore or fatigued, cut that easy run duration by about 25 to 50 percent.” If you’re experiencing pain that affects your stride, however, it’s better to stop immediately rather than push through.

It’s also worth paying attention to how you feel after your recovery run.

For Mackey, the biggest giveaway that an athlete isn’t recovering adequately is often what happens during their next hard workout. “If they’re struggling to hit their usual paces, feeling unusually fatigued, or showing a noticeable drop in motivation, I know it’s time to reassess their recovery sessions,” he notes.

It has been revealed that if these warning signs persist, the best option might just be skipping your next recovery run altogether. A rest day, walk, or low-impact cross-training session can give your body a break from the repetitive loading of running, particularly when you’re dealing with lingering fatigue.

And if you think cutting a run short feels like a missed training opportunity, take a cue from the pros: “This is one of the biggest differences I see in elite runners,” notes Fitzgerald. “They take pride in their restraint and ability to hold back, because they know it’s part of a more intentional plan.”.

Wilde Wins Second Race of Weekend as Taylor-Brown Takes Down Derron at T100 Dubai

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Less than 24 hours after his third-place finish at WTCS Abu Dhabi, Hayden Wilde (NZL) showed few outward signs of fatigue as he hit the front of the race in T1, rode among the leaders, and ran his way to victory ahead of training partner Kyle Smith (NZL).
  • Industry observers note that georgia Taylor-Brown said before the race that she wanted to “beat Julie,” and her wish came true.
  • It was a mixed cast of T100 veterans and rookies on the men’s start line, with several notable names absent after the men’s Saudi Arabia T100 race was moved to Dubai on short notice.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Less than 24 hours after his third-place finish at WTCS Abu Dhabi, Hayden Wilde (NZL) showed few outward signs of fatigue as he hit the front of the race in T1, rode among the leaders, and ran his way to victory ahead of training partner Kyle Smith (NZL).

Industry observers note that georgia Taylor-Brown said before the race that she wanted to “beat Julie,” and her wish came true. A small breakaway in the swim put Derron (SUI) on the back foot from the start, while Taylor-Brown had to overcome cramps on the bike and a charging Nicole Van Der Kaay (NZL) on the run to earn a narrow, yet important victory.

It was a mixed cast of T100 veterans and rookies on the men’s start line, with several notable names absent after the men’s Saudi Arabia T100 race was moved to Dubai on short notice.

Big news leading into the race was that RaceRanger devices would not be used on the bike due to customs delays in getting the equipment into Dubai, leaving officials to enforce the 20-meter draft zone without the light sensor system.

Recent findings suggest that A large group emerged from the tepid water to start the bike. After a subpar swim left Wilde chasing in Abu Dhabi the day before, he not only swam with the front group but sprinted through transition, smiling and chatting as he rounded Rico Bogen (GER), showing little sign of the previous day’s effort.

He took his time putting on full-length aero socks as Menno Koolhaas (NED) went straight to the front to lead the men onto the scorching tarmac for 80km of time trialing on the flat course.

The group of 17 after the swim rapidly whittled down to 10 as average speeds approached 30 mph in the opening stages.

In a recent development, as Bogen, Wilde, and Smith continued to push the pace, the group rapidly dropped to just six. The standout name among the group was Mika Noodt (GER), back racing for the first time since his collision with an ambulance at Ironman 70.3 Swansea in July and already taking turns at the front.

Noodt had been one of the sport’s biggest up-and-coming stars before the accident and was to be Wilde’s strongest challenger on the T100 circuit this year. He has openly shared the mental struggles and trauma that followed the crash, but it seemed he was back to full strength on course as the German powered toward the run.

Off the bike, a quick transition saw Wilde round Bogen for the lead, and he looked set to run away without a challenge. Smith, however, quickly moved alongside him and stayed there for the opening laps until Wilde turned up the heat.

According to recent reports, from there, there was no stopping him as he put last year’s lap-counting drama in Dubai behind him to head into the Qatar final with a perfect score from his three counting results. Smith held on for his best T100 result of the year, ahead of an emotional Noodt, who marked his return with an immediate trip to the podium.

One of the most remarkable revelations came afterward, when Wilde shared that he believed he had raced much of the day with a broken toe. He injured it during the Aussie exit on the swim and, thinking it might be dislocated, tried to pop it back into place during the bike. Despite the swelling afterward, he stated it had not troubled him too much on the run.

A front group of four broke away early on the swim as Taylor-Brown and Kate Waugh’s (GBR) proposal to put Derron under pressure from the start worked perfectly. Waugh led through the Aussie exit before Sara Pérez Sala (ESP) led the group into T1.

Derron found herself almost a minute down, but alongside strong riders Caroline Pohle (GER) and Van der Kaay, she remained well within contention. The substantial question was whether her efforts in Kona would affect her race or whether the heat preparation would prove beneficial in the sweltering conditions.

On the bike, it appeared to be the former as Pohle and Van der Kaay left her behind and worked their way to the front. They eventually helped put more time into Derron, who was over two minutes back and still losing ground on the third lap.

It was not an unfamiliar position for Derron, who had overcome a deficit at the previous women’s race in Vancouver to take down Taylor-Brown and Waugh.

According to recent reports, however, it soon became clear that only Taylor-Brown would remain in the fight for the win, with Waugh’s race unraveling in the heat. She later shared on social media that she had started the race sick but still managed to get across the line in ninth, her first T100 finish off the podium.

It has been revealed that everything was going according to strategy for Taylor-Brown until she began suffering from adductor cramps late on the bike. She lost positions as she tried to soft-pedal them out, but thankfully for her, they subsided enough for her to start the run just 36 seconds behind Pohle, with Van der Kaay and Pérez Sala also ahead.

Industry observers note that taylor-Brown’s cramps were well in her rearview as she quickly made up the gap and began building a lead. By the third lap, it looked as though that advantage might continue to grow all the way to the finish.

However, Van der Kaay was putting together the best T100 performance of her career and began closing again heading into the final lap. Derron had moved into third but was not making any significant inroads into either athlete ahead.

It has been revealed that van der Kaay put in one final surge to try to catch Taylor-Brown but came up just 10 seconds short. The victory now sends Taylor-Brown into the Grand Final six points clear of Derron and in pole position to become world champion.

Van der Kaay’s excellent performance, which included the second-fastest bike and third-fastest run, moves her into third in the standings heading into the final.

3 Restorative Yoga Poses for When You’re Stressed and Short on Time

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In Yoga Journal’s Archives series, we share a curated collection of articles originally published in past issues beginning in 1975. This article about restorative yoga poses appeared in the September-October 1995 issue of Yoga Journal. Find more of our Archives here.

In a perfect world we would all have time for a long restorative yoga practice daily. But obligations to work, family, friends, and community often leave us with little time for self-care. It is precisely when we are the most stressed that we need to relax and renew ourselves, and bring some restorative yoga into our busy lives.

In a recent development, traditionally, a yoga class or personal practice session begins with active poses followed by a brief restorative pose. However, the entire focus of this practice is on supported restorative poses.

It has been revealed that to relax deeply in this amount of time, you must have a quiet room, but you can get by with a minimum of props. There are only three poses: Legs-Up-the-Wall Pose, Supported Child’s Pose, and Basic Relaxation Pose. Practice them in the order presented. If you can’t find even 15 minutes, practice Basic Relaxation Pose for five.

In a recent development, this pose is simple to practice, even when traveling. Just lie on your back and let a nearby wall support your legs. This pose brings the blood and lymph fluid to pool in the abdomen, refreshing the leg muscles and enhancing the health of the circulatory system. In addition, the pose reverses the energy of the legs from moving down and out to the feet, as in our normal stance, to moving down and back to the pelvis. Nothing feels better to tired legs and feet than being elevated.

Recent findings suggest that setting Up. To begin, sit on the floor with one shoulder near the wall and your thighs parallel to the wall. Roll back as you swing your legs up the wall. Once in position, make sure that your lower back is not rounded and your tailbone and buttocks are not lifting off the floor. If they are, move slightly away from the wall so your lower back is comfortably supported by the floor.

If your chin lifts toward the ceiling, place a standard-fold blanket under your head and neck to support your cervical curve. Make sure your chin is slightly lower than your forehead, but do not force your chin down and flatten the back of your neck.

Keep your legs straight but relaxed. Place your arms out to your sides with the palms turned up. Close your eyes. Place an eyebag over them.

Being There. Take several long, slow breaths. As you do, imagine the fluid in your legs flowing down toward the abdomen. With it, all tension drains out of your legs. They begin to feel lighter and softer. Imagine that your brain is shrinking in size as it moves away from your forehead and sinks toward the back of your head and the floor. Feel your entire spine supported by the floor. The position of the arms creates a feeling of being open and free. Enjoy this feeling.

In a recent development, coming Back. Practice Legs-Up-the-Wall Pose for five minutes. When ready, remove the eyebag and open your eyes. Rest for a few breaths before bending your knees toward your chest and rolling to one side. Pause again for a few breaths before slowly coming to a sitting position with the help of your arms.

Recent findings suggest that benefits. Legs-Up-the-Wall Pose reduces swelling and fatigue in the legs.

Cautions: Do not practice this inverted pose.

Supported Child’s Pose is the familiar posture of rest and sleep for babies and young children. When you practice this pose, not only will it help to relieve tension in your lower back, but it may evoke a sense of security from your earliest days. This pose is one of introversion, one of curling up and reconnecting with feelings of support and release.

Sources indicate that setting Up. Begin by kneeling on a carpeted floor or blanket with your knees hip-width apart and your bolster in front of you. Use more padding under your knees and shins if you need it. To avoid stress on the ligaments of your outer ankles, point your toes directly backward and not toward each other. Sit back on your heels.

Industry observers note that if you experience discomfort in your knees, ankles, or tops of your feet, come up and try one or both of the following adjustments. Place one towel, folded lengthwise, into the bend of your knees to create more space in the knee joints. Place the other towel, rolled lengthwise, under the front of the ankles, and let your feet hang over the roll. Experiment with the thickness of these folded and rolled towels to get them just right for you.

Recent findings suggest that sit back on your heels again. Separate your knees wide enough to place the bolster between your thighs. To enhance relaxation, hold a sandbag across your lower back as you bend forward. The weight of the bag helps to relax the muscles of your lower back.

Industry observers note that your torso should be completely supported by the bolster and your thighs. Your chest should rest easily on the bolster. Let your tailbone drop toward your heels. This action will lengthen your lower back as you relax. Your buttocks do not have to touch your heels.

If you need more support, try one of the following variations. Come up to a kneeling position and place a long-roll blanket on your heels and sit back, or come to a kneeling position and significantly raise the height of your torso support by adding one or more single-fold blankets. If you have difficulty breathing, push the bolster forward so it only supports your breastbone and lets your belly hang free.

Industry observers note that turn your head to one side and bring your chin slightly toward your chest. Turn it to the opposite side halfway through the practice of Supported Child’s Pose. If the side head position is uncomfortable, rest on your forehead and slightly tuck your chin toward your chest. Make sure you can breathe easily regardless of your head position.

Place your arms so they reach either back toward your feet or forward around the edges of the bolster. The position of the arms is unimportant; it is notable that you are comfortable. Close your eyes.

Being There. Take several slow breaths. As you do, let your shoulders move away from the ears. Let your belly relax and feel supported. The counter-pressure of the bolster on the belly may feel especially good if you have menstrual cramps.

Coming Back. Practice Supported Child’s Pose for three minutes. Be sure that you spend equal time with your head turned in both directions. Open your eyes. Reach back with one hand and slide the sandbag off your back and to one side. Place your palms on the floor, under your shoulders. Press your hands into the floor, inhale, and sit up slowly onto your heels. Rest for a moment. Come to a kneeling position and immediately bring one leg forward, placing your foot on the floor. Press your hands on the forward thigh, and inhale deeply as you come to a standing position. Coming out of the pose in this way prevents discomfort in the knees.

According to recent reports, benefits. Supported Child’s Pose gently stretches the lower back, relieves shoulder tension, and quiets the mind.

Cautions: Do not practice this pose.

Industry observers note that this pose is the heart of restorative practice. Relaxing completely, even if it is only for five minutes, is one of the most vital skills you can acquire. When you have learned to relax whenever and wherever you need to, you can use this skill in a variety of situations to reduce stress and its accompanying fatigue.

According to recent reports, the less time you think you have for spending a few minutes a day in Basic Relaxation Pose, the more you need to do it. If you do nothing else for your health every day, make time for this pose. Practice it, for example, at an afternoon break at work, when you first come home from work, after a workout session, or whenever you feel depleted, exhausted, or stressed.

Sources indicate that setting Up. In Basic Relaxation Pose you will be lying on your back with your arms out to the sides and your legs comfortably apart. Give yourself enough floor space to spread out comfortably. Before you lie down, position a standard-fold blanket for your head and neck to rest on.

Begin by sitting on the floor. If you have a tendency to get cold, cover your legs with an unfolded blanket. Now turn to one side and lean on your elbow and forearm as you slide onto your side. Then roll onto your back. Coming into the pose in this way is less stressful on your back than leaning back into a reclining position.

It has been revealed that roll the long edge of your standard-fold blanket slightly to support the gentle curve of the neck. Adjust the prop placement so that your neck is comfortable. Your chin should be slightly lower than your forehead. This position quiets the frontal lobes of the brain. If you are using an extra blanket for warmth, now is the time to pull it up to cover your torso and arms. Cover your eyes with an eyebag.

Many people can practice this pose lying flat on the floor. If you have tension or pain in your abdomen or lower back, place a long-roll blanket under the backs of your knees before you lie down. Make sure that your legs are relaxed and the knees supported by the long-roll blanket. If your heels do not touch the floor, place a folded blanket or pillow under them. If your lower back discomfort persists, come out of the pose by following the instructions under Coming Back (below). Resume your practice of Basic Relaxation Pose when you feel ready.

According to recent reports, once you have established yourself, observe the position of your body. Your arms and legs should be equidistant from an imaginary line drawn from the tip of your nose to exactly midway between the feet. Most people practice with the palms turned upwards, but if this is not comfortable, turn them down and let the elbows relax. The most notable thing is that you feel completely at ease and supported by the props and the floor. If you need to sit up to adjust props and lie down again, follow the instructions for Coming Back and Setting Up.

Sources indicate that being There. Swallow and relax your lower jaw. Soften your upper eyelids and look down toward the lower lids as you close your eyes. Let your cheeks feel hollow and loose beneath the cheekbones. Release the root of your tongue. Your fingers will curl naturally as your hands relax. Let your legs roll outward. Allow the entire back of your body to feel at ease and in complete contact with the floor and the props.

Your arms and legs will feel longer and longer, as well as heavier. Feel the large muscles of the legs, buttocks, and trunk drop away from the bones. Now feel the smaller muscles of your arms, neck, and head as they seem to move away from the bones. Let the bones themselves feel heavy and the skin loose, all over your body. Notice that the abdominal organs seem to nestle gently back into your body. Savor the silence.

The Centering Breath. As you continue to rest, notice when you begin to feel lighter. This is a signal that your body has relaxed and that you can begin the Centering Breath: a long inhalation followed by a long exhalation, followed by several cycles of normal breathing.

In a recent development, begin by slowly inviting the inhalation to move more deeply into your body. Do this by lifting your ribs slightly and spreading your lungs. Let the air come to you. As you inhale, imagine that the breath breathes you. Follow the inhalation with a soft focus on the exhalation. Feel your diaphragm, lungs, ribs, and muscles of respiration contracting to press the breath out in a steady and focused stream. When your exhalation is finished, breathe several normal cycles of inhalation and exhalation.

In a recent development, then inhale slowly and deeply once again. At the fullness of inhalation, pause slightly before melting the inhalation into an equally long and steady exhalation. The inhalation is the receptive part of the breath; the exhalation is the active part. Once again, take several normal cycles of breath.

Once you have established the rhythm of the long breaths, pay particular attention to the quality of these breaths. What is their texture? Is the beginning of inhalation as soft as the end of inhalation? Is the end of exhalation as smooth as the beginning? With each cycle, allow your breath to become more and more refined, like the texture of fine silk.

Remember, never strain or force the breath. If at any time you feel even slightly agitated or out of breath, simply return to normal breathing. Once you feel calm, resume the cycle of long, slow inhalation and exhalation, followed by several normal breaths.

It has been revealed that the success of the Centering Breath is not measured by how much air you can take in or let out. So go slowly, gently, and be present with the process. If you feel fatigued, anxious, or light-headed during practice, it is an indication that you have practiced long enough. Let your breathing return to normal, and, in the future, take longer breaks of normal breathing between each round of long inhalation and long exhalation. Do not practice the Centering Breath if you have a fever, a bad cold, sinusitis, or more serious respiratory diseases, such as pneumonia.

In a recent development, repeat the Centering Breath for up to 10 rounds. Be sure to leave some time for normal breathing before coming out of the pose.

Industry observers note that coming Back. Remain in Basic Relaxation Pose for five to 20 minutes. To come out of the pose, bend one knee and roll onto your side. Let the eyebag fall off by itself. Gradually open your eyes. Rest in this position for a few breaths. To sit up, press the floor with the elbow of your lower arm and the palm of the hand of your upper arm. Sit quietly for several breaths before standing up and resuming your normal activities.

Benefits. Basic Relaxation Pose lowers blood pressure and heart rate, releases muscular tension, reduces fatigue, improves sleep, enhances immune response, and helps to manage chronic pain.

Research Shows This Is the Best Way to Balance Strength Training and Running

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1243 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Runnersworld

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, there’s a reason why run coaches and personal trainers emphasize strength training in addition to running: Practicing both forms of exercise will allow you to build stronger muscles and increase your aerobic capacity at the same time.
  • Industry observers note that but sometimes, especially after a heavy leg day workout, your body can feel pretty tired and sore and seemingly not ready to take on miles.
  • In a recent development, so if you’ve ever been tempted to skip the weights today in favor of a better run tomorrow, consider the advantages of strength training.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, there’s a reason why run coaches and personal trainers emphasize strength training in addition to running: Practicing both forms of exercise will allow you to build stronger muscles and increase your aerobic capacity at the same time. Combining strength training and a running schedule means you boost your fitness in multiple ways.

Industry observers note that but sometimes, especially after a heavy leg day workout, your body can feel pretty tired and sore and seemingly not ready to take on miles. This isn’t just in your head. According to a review of 132 studies, it takes a full day or two more to recover from resistance training than it does a high-intensity run.

In a recent development, so if you’ve ever been tempted to skip the weights today in favor of a better run tomorrow, consider the advantages of strength training. Not only does it just feel good to move your muscles through full ranges of motion, especially after sitting all day, but it can also pay off in the long run for your run performance and overall health. In fact, several studies point to better running economy, as well as VO2 max and anaerobic threshold, when following a program that incorporates both endurance training and strength training.

According to recent reports, instead of ditching strength exercises to focus on mileage, the key is creating a strength training schedule that optimally fits into your run training. After all, strength training is supposed to help, not harm, your running. Here’s how to achieve that.

Industry observers note that get the strength plan that works for all runners! Race-Ready Strength, our fresh progressive 4-week training program, will get you in the best shape to reach your racing goals.

To get it right, you need to understand how your body reacts to moving heavy stuff. Picture pushing a hand truck 50 feet. Pretty easy. That’s running—your body is the hand truck and it moves its own weight rather effortlessly. Now slide the hand truck under a fridge and push it just five feet. A lot more difficult. That’s mechanical loading; it’s why 10 heavy squats feels so much more challenging than 1,000 foot strikes.

The reason strength training makes you faster is because it lowers the amount of energy required to hit a certain pace, explains Kenji Doma, Ph.D., a sports and exercise scientist at James Cook University in Queensland, Australia, and author of a 2014 study on strength training and running performance published in the European Journal of Sports Science.

Recent findings suggest that doma has also studied the effects of combining aerobic exercise and strength training on muscle hypertrophy and strength, as published in a Sports Medicine systematic review and meta-analysis in 2022. The researchers found that combining the two types of training doesn’t hinder strength and muscle-building gains, but can compromise explosive strength gains when performed in the same session—something to consider if that’s your goal.

What’s crucial to note is that when you lift weights, your brain alters its neural recruitment pattern, calling up the most fatigue-resistant muscle fibers so you exert less energy. That’s why you don’t want to skimp on strength training. Doma’s research offers guidance on how best to combine mile repeats and repetitions in the gym for a more well-rounded running and strength training schedule.

In the study that focused specifically on running performance, 15 runners of a wide range of ability and average weekly mileage did different strength-training sessions on three occasions. One workout was a high-intensity, total-body session, one was high intensity but for legs only, and one was a low-intensity, total-body workout.

In a recent development, six hours after each workout, the runners did a treadmill test for 10 minutes at 70 percent of ventilatory threshold pace (easy), then 10 minutes at 90 percent of threshold pace (roughly close to half marathon pace), and then as long as possible at 110 percent of threshold pace. The runners also did the treadmill test at the outset of the study, to get a benchmark for how they would perform when fresh.

Industry observers note that the high-intensity strength workouts significantly lessened the runners’ time to exhaustion at the end of the treadmill test. In the benchmark test, they’d lasted an average of close to five minutes at 110 percent of threshold pace. After each of the high-intensity strength sessions, time to exhaustion was almost a minute less, suggesting that the hard weight workouts six hours earlier had dramatically decreased the runners’ ability to sustain fast running.

Doma says his findings have practical implications for how runners should arrange their workouts.

Sources indicate that first, he advises not to schedule a hard running workout later in the day of a weight session. “Running at maximal effort is impaired six hours [after] lower-extremity resistance training, and therefore trained to moderately-trained runners will need more than that to recover for running sessions set at high intensities,” he states.

Plus, running at maximal effort is still impaired 24 hours after lower-extremity resistance training, according to Doma. “Therefore, in the case of trained and moderately-trained runners undertaking high-intensity running sessions after lower-extremity resistance training, they may need more than one day to recover.”.

Doma also found that running performance at lower intensities was unaffected by the weight workouts. “Runners could undertake strength training and running sessions on the same day six hours apart as long as the running session is set at submaximal intensities,” Doma says. In other words, if you have an easy, long run, or recovery run on the schedule, it’ll be fine to double up that day, as long as workouts are more than six hours apart.

Industry observers note that if possible, Doma suggests arranging your schedule so that on days that you run and lift, running comes first. “I found that lower-extremity resistance training performed six hours prior to running sessions at moderate to high intensities cause carryover effects of fatigue the next day to a greater extent than the reverse sequence,” he states. “Therefore, if undertaking lower-extremity resistance training and running sessions on the same day, it is best to undertake a running session before a strength training session. For example, running in the morning before work and lower-extremity resistance training in the evening after work.”.

In this scenario, it would make sense to have that morning run be one of your harder workouts of the week. Your workout the following day would then be an easy recovery run, which would be warranted even without the evening lifting, but is that much more called for on the basis of Doma’s research.

This sequence would also mesh with many coaches’ recommendation to have great discrepancy between your hard and easy days, so that you can better recover from your toughest workouts—instead of including hard elements of non-running training on your easy running days.

Scott is a veteran running, fitness, and health journalist who has held senior editorial positions at Runner’s World and Running Times. Much of his writing translates sport science research and elite best practices into practical guidance for everyday athletes. He is the author or coauthor of several running books, including Running Is My Therapy, Advanced Marathoning, and Meb for Mortals. Scott has also written about running for Slate, The Atlantic, the Washington Post, and other members of the sedentary media. His lifetime running odometer is past 110,000 miles, but he’s as much in love as ever.
